I continued to read chapter four, which cataloged the various performance venues I had played in during my twenties. I saved the document to my hard drive.

We entered the restaurant and the host guided us to a table near the back wall. The menus placed before us were printed entirely in Vietnamese. I opened my menu and began scanning the options. I offered to translate the items for my partner, Taylor. Taylor declined the offer and stated that translation was not required. I inquired why that was the case. Taylor told me about a daily language class attended during lunch breaks. "I can read the descriptions of the noodle dishes," Taylor said. Taylor pointed to a specific item on the page and read the ingredients aloud in Vietnamese. The pronunciation was functional. I confirmed that the translation was accurate. The waiter arrived at the table with a notepad. Taylor ordered the dish by speaking its Vietnamese name. The waiter wrote it down and collected our menus.

Priya was placing folded shirts into her suitcase when she noticed a small, blue paperback book sitting on the nightstand. The title indicated it was a conversational Hindi phrasebook. Her partner, Rohan, entered the bedroom carrying a pair of shoes. Priya picked up the book and asked him if it belonged to him. Rohan confirmed that it did. He explained that he had been studying Hindi grammar and vocabulary since they booked their upcoming trip. "I wanted to be able to communicate with your relatives without relying on you to translate," Rohan said. Priya opened the book and saw that multiple pages were highlighted with a yellow marker. She pointed out that the formal conjugation was necessary when speaking to her grandparents. Rohan nodded and asked her to demonstrate the correct phrasing. Priya spoke the sentence, and Rohan repeated it.

Elena entered the home office to retrieve a pen from the desk drawer. Next to the keyboard, there was a notebook left open to a middle page. The page contained lists of Cyrillic letters alongside their English phonetic translations. Tom walked in holding a stack of mail. Elena held up the notebook and inquired about the handwriting. Tom said that he enrolled in an online Russian course in January. "You have filled half of this notebook with vocabulary," Elena noted. Tom confirmed this and added that he was currently learning how to conjugate verbs in the past tense. He set the mail on the desk and asked if she wanted to read his recent assignment. Elena read the short paragraph written in Russian. She pointed out a grammatical error in the second sentence. Tom took a pencil and corrected the mistake.

I sat at the table nearest the window while David went to the counter to order our beverages. The barista asked him for our order. Instead of speaking English, David replied in Arabic. He requested two black coffees and a pastry. I watched the exchange from my seat. When David returned to the table and set the tray down, I mentioned that he had just spoken my native language. He told me he hired a tutor three months ago and attends sessions twice a week. "Your pronunciation of the consonants was accurate," I said. He picked up his cup and took a drink of the coffee. He explained that his tutor provided audio recordings to assist with his accent. We remained at the table for another twenty minutes before leaving the café to walk back to the apartment.

Mark walked into the kitchen and picked up Sarah’s phone to check the time. The screen was unlocked, displaying an application for language acquisition. The current lesson was on Tagalog verb conjugations. Sarah entered the room and set a grocery bag on the counter. Mark pointed to the screen and asked why she was studying Tagalog. She stated that she had been spending thirty minutes a day on the application for the past four months. Mark listened as she proceeded to recite a list of basic vocabulary words, including the terms for household items and days of the week. He placed the phone back on the counter. "I can help you practice pronunciation if you want," he said. Sarah nodded and began unpacking the groceries, placing the canned goods in the pantry and the vegetables in the refrigerator.

I stood at the counter in the post office while my partner, Jordan, filled out a customs declaration form for a package. I looked over at the envelope resting on the scale. The destination address was in Paris, directed to my aunt. I noticed that the brief message written on the outside of the envelope was in French. I asked Jordan about the text. Jordan informed me of a daily routine involving online language tutorials over the past year. "I wrote a short greeting to your aunt in the letter as well," Jordan added. I asked what the greeting said. Jordan recited the French sentences, which detailed our recent move to a new apartment. The grammar was largely correct, with one error in noun gender. I pointed out the error. Jordan noted the correction. We paid for the postage and left.

I stood in the reference aisle of the bookstore while my wife, Chloe, browsed the foreign language section. She approached me carrying a children's book written entirely in Greek. I pointed to the cover and noted that the text was in my native language. Chloe informed me that she had been studying Greek grammar using a software program. "I decided to purchase a book to practice my reading comprehension," she said. I opened the book to the first page and read the text aloud. I asked her to translate the sentence. Chloe identified the subject and the verb, then provided an English translation that matched the text. I closed the book and handed it back to her. She carried the item to the cash register and completed the transaction. We exited the store and walked toward the parking garage.

Lin set the laptop on the dining table and initiated a video call with her parents in Beijing. Her partner, James, pulled out a chair and sat next to her. When Lin's parents appeared on the screen, James greeted them in Mandarin. Lin turned her head and looked at him. She asked him how he knew that specific greeting. James replied that he had hired a tutor. He then looked back at the screen and asked Lin's parents about the weather in Beijing, using Mandarin. Lin's father responded that it was currently raining. James translated the response into English for Lin, though she already understood. "Your tones are quite precise," Lin said to James. He acknowledged the statement and proceeded to ask her mother what they were having for dinner. The video call lasted for an additional forty-five minutes.

I reached into the pocket of my husband’s coat to retrieve the car keys. Instead of keys, my fingers grasped a stack of index cards. I pulled them out and saw German vocabulary words written on one side and English translations on the other. Michael walked out of the library carrying three hardcover books. I showed him the index cards and asked him about them. He told me he made the flashcards two weeks ago. "I memorize ten new words each morning while eating breakfast," Michael said. I flipped through the stack and found the card for the word associated with a library. I asked him to pronounce it. He recited the German word. I told him the vowel sound needed to be longer. He repeated the word, elongating the vowel. I returned the cards to his coat pocket.

Ji-Woo and Liam sat on the sofa to watch a film. The movie was a Korean production. Ji-Woo reached for the remote to turn on the English subtitles. Liam placed his hand over the remote and said that the subtitles were unnecessary. Ji-Woo asked if he would be able to understand the dialogue without them. Liam explained that he had been taking a Korean language class at the community center on Tuesday evenings. He stated that his comprehension level was sufficient for basic conversations. "We can turn the subtitles back on if the vocabulary gets too complex," Liam added. Ji-Woo pressed the play button. They watched the screen for an hour. When a character in the film asked for directions to the train station, Liam translated the response into English. Ji-Woo nodded and continued watching the movie until the credits rolled.

Carlos and Sofia were walking along the paved path in the municipal park. Carlos’s phone vibrated in his jacket. He pulled it out and looked at the screen. The text message was from Sofia, despite her walking beside him. The message was written in Spanish, asking what time they should head back to the apartment. Carlos stopped walking and asked her when she started writing in Spanish. Sofia stated that she had been studying the language for six months using digital textbooks. "I downloaded a Spanish keyboard on my phone yesterday," she said. Carlos typed a response in Spanish, suggesting they leave in ten minutes. Sofia read the reply on her screen and verbally agreed. They resumed their walk, following the path until it looped back to the parking lot where their vehicle was parked. They got into the car.

We were driving on the interstate when my partner, Alex, connected a phone to the car's audio system. An instructional podcast began playing. The speaker in the audio gave instructions on Swahili sentence structure. I looked at Alex and asked when the lessons had started. Alex kept both hands on the steering wheel and stated that the audio series was a recent purchase. "I listen to it during my daily commute," Alex said. I listened to the next five minutes of the podcast, which covered the vocabulary for different types of weather. The narrator prompted the listener to repeat the phrases. Alex repeated the Swahili phrase for heavy rain. I corrected the emphasis on the second syllable. Alex repeated the phrase again with the adjustment. We drove the remaining forty miles to the destination with the podcast continuing to play through the speakers.

Arthur wore his rental shoes and stood at lane four. His brother, Thomas, was sitting at the scoring console. Thomas informed Arthur that the surprise bowling party was cancelled because the facility double-booked the lanes. "A league tournament begins in fifteen minutes," Thomas said. He added that the rest of their friends were instructed to stay home. Arthur looked at the scoreboard, which displayed a blank grid. "I will return the shoes to the front desk," Arthur said. Thomas unlaced his own rental shoes and placed them in a plastic bin. He told Arthur that the deposit had already been refunded to his credit card. "We need to leave before the tournament players arrive," Thomas said. Arthur carried the shoes to the counter and handed them to the employee.

I parked my vehicle at the beach access point and walked down the wooden boardwalk. A fire pit was dug into the sand, surrounded by six folding chairs. My colleague, Rachel, was extinguishing the embers with a bucket of seawater. She told me that the surprise bonfire for my promotion was cancelled due to the strict municipal fire ban that went into effect at noon. "The park ranger issued a warning," Rachel said. I asked if the others had already left the beach. Rachel said that they returned to their cars five minutes ago. "I will carry these chairs back to my truck," I said. I folded three of the chairs and tucked them under my arms. Rachel poured the remaining water into the pit. "We must leave no trace," she said.

Lydia unlocked the door to her ceramics studio and turned on the overhead lights. A large cake box sat on the potter’s wheel. Her studio partner, Julian, was wiping down the countertops with a damp rag. Julian stated that the surprise gallery reception they had organized for her was cancelled. "The gallery owner lost the keys to the main exhibition space," Julian said. He explained that no one could get inside the building. Lydia looked at the cake box. "I will put the cake in the refrigerator," she said. Julian nodded and rinsed the rag in the sink. He mentioned that the event would not be rescheduled this month. "I need to start glazing these bowls," Lydia said. She opened the refrigerator door, placed the box on the top shelf, and closed it.

I drove up the gravel road and parked next to the rented cabin. My cousin, Sarah, was standing on the porch holding a clipboard. She informed me that my surprise weekend getaway was cancelled because the cabin's heating system was broken. "The temperature inside is forty degrees," Sarah said. She noted that she had already called the rental company. I asked if the other family members were en route. Sarah told me that they turned their cars around after she called them. "I will keep the engine running," I said. Sarah walked down the wooden steps and opened the passenger door of my car. She said that she needed to drop off the cabin keys at the main office. I shifted the car into reverse and backed down the gravel driveway.

Dr. Aris swiped his keycard and entered the laboratory. A sign that read "Congratulations on the Grant" was resting on the floor near the centrifuge. A technician named Robert was removing a tray of cupcakes from a sterile counter. Robert told Dr. Aris that the surprise celebration was cancelled because a Level 2 contamination protocol had been initiated in the adjacent room. "Security requires the floor to be evacuated," Robert said. He explained that the cupcakes had to be discarded. "I will power down the microscopes," Dr. Aris said. Robert threw the baked goods into the biohazard disposal bin. He said that the evacuation alarm would sound in two minutes. "Make sure to log out of the main terminal," Robert said. Dr. Aris pressed the power button on the computer and waited for the screen to go black.

I walked into the gymnasium of the local community center. The bleachers were pulled out, and several folding tables were stacked against the far wall. The facility manager approached me with a clipboard. He informed me that the surprise retirement party my neighbors planned was cancelled. "The roof has a structural leak," he said, pointing to a puddle in the center of the basketball court. He added that the building inspector closed the gymnasium for the weekend. I told him that I understood the situation. "I will notify the delivery driver to halt the catering," I said. The manager nodded and wrote something on his paper. He said that the front doors would be locked at three o'clock. "I am leaving now," I said. I turned and walked out through the double doors.

I stepped into the Italian restaurant and walked to the back room. The tables were pushed together, and a single balloon was tied to the back of a chair. The manager approached me and stated that the reservation for my surprise dinner had been cancelled by my sister. "She called ten minutes ago to say the flight was delayed," the manager said. He asked if I still wanted a table for one. I told him that I would eat at the bar instead. "You can sit at the corner stool," the manager said. I sat down and placed my jacket on the adjacent seat. The bartender handed me a menu and a glass of water. I read the list of appetizers. The manager removed the balloon from the chair and carried it to the kitchen.

I entered the rare books reading room at the public library. A group of chairs was arranged in a circle, and a wrapped gift sat on the central table. My supervisor, Mr. Vance, was shelving a stack of reference books. He informed me that the surprise ten-year work anniversary party was cancelled. "The head librarian enacted a strict noise ordinance for today," Mr. Vance said. He explained that a lecture was being recorded in the next room. I stated that I would return the chairs to their original positions. "The gift is a new fountain pen," Mr. Vance said. He instructed me to take it to my desk. I picked up the box and placed it in my pocket. "I will start my shift at the circulation desk," I said, pushing a chair to the wall.

Maya took the elevator to the rooftop garden of her apartment building. A long table was covered with unused plates and a stack of napkins. Her neighbor, Kevin, was untying a cluster of balloons from the railing. Kevin told Maya that the surprise rooftop party for her anniversary was cancelled due to a wind advisory. "The gusts are measuring over forty miles per hour," Kevin said. He stated that the property management requested the roof be cleared. "I will carry the plates back down to my kitchen," Maya said. Kevin handed her the stack of plates and told her to watch her step. "Hold the door for me," Kevin said as he gathered the balloons. Maya walked to the stairwell and pulled the heavy metal door open, waiting for Kevin to pass through.

Elena arrived at the pavilion in the city park at noon. Two wooden picnic tables were covered with plastic tablecloths, but the area was otherwise empty. Greg was packing a stack of plastic cups into a cardboard box. He told Elena that the surprise picnic for her graduation was cancelled because the forecast predicted heavy rain within the hour. "I will help you load the boxes into the trunk of your car," Elena said. Greg handed her a cooler filled with ice and canned beverages. He said that he had sent a mass text message to the invitees. "Let's move quickly," Greg said. Elena carried the cooler across the grass to the parking lot. She placed it into the trunk. Drops of water began to fall on the windshield as Greg closed the trunk lid.

I opened the door to my apartment at six in the evening. My roommate, David, was sweeping up confetti from the hardwood floor. He mentioned that the surprise party they had planned for me was no longer happening. "The plumbing issue in the bathroom requires immediate repair," David said, pointing his broom toward the hallway. A plumber was currently working on the pipes. David explained that the guests had been notified not to arrive. "I will put the chairs back in the dining room," I said. David nodded and deposited the swept confetti into the trash can. I carried three folding chairs from the living room to the table. The sound of a wrench hitting metal came from the hallway. "The plumber needs more towels," David said. I walked to the linen closet to retrieve them.

Mark walked into the breakroom at 4:00 PM. A banner reading "Happy Birthday Mark" was folded on the table next to a stack of paper plates. Susan stood by the refrigerator taking down streamers. She turned and looked at him. Susan said that the gathering had been called off due to the scheduling conflict with the mandatory staff meeting. "I will inform the caterer to cancel the sandwich order," Mark said. Susan placed the streamers into the recycling bin. She told him that she had already called the vendor. Mark nodded and picked up his coffee mug from the counter. "I am returning to my desk," he said. Susan closed the refrigerator door. The overhead fluorescent lights hummed as Mark walked out of the room, leaving the folded banner beside the paper plates.

Greg read the notification from the genealogy app while commuting on the morning train. The app identified a biological mother and father living in a different state from his family. He composed a text message to his mother asking about the discrepancy. She called him three minutes later. "We adopted you in 1995," she said over the phone. Greg asked if she knew the names listed on the app. She stated she had never met the biological parents because it was a closed arrangement. "I will need to review the adoption decree," Greg said. She told him the decree was filed at the county courthouse. Greg acknowledged the information and ended the call. The train arrived at his station. He placed his phone in his briefcase, stood up, and exited the train car onto the platform.

The notification appeared on my tablet while I drank my coffee. The ancestry website updated my profile with a list of close relatives. The names listed under the immediate family section were unfamiliar. I showed the screen to my father, who sat across the table. "Look at these results," I said. He put on his reading glasses and looked at the tablet. He then stated that he and my mother had adopted me from an orphanage in Seattle thirty years ago. I asked him why he had not mentioned it previously. He replied that the topic simply had not come up in conversation. "Please send me the details of the orphanage," I said. He nodded and wrote down the name on a napkin. I paid the bill for the coffee, took the napkin, and we walked to the parking lot.

Dr. Aris examined her personal genotype sequencing on the laboratory monitor. The data showed haplogroups that diverged entirely from her documented maternal and paternal lineages. She picked up her office phone and called her father's residential facility. When the nurse handed him the receiver, Aris informed him that her sequence showed no biological connection. "We adopted you when you were four months old," her father said. Aris asked him to provide the location of her birth. He told her she was born in a hospital in Vancouver. "I will need the exact name of the hospital for my records," Aris said. He stated he would mail her the documents by the end of the week. Aris thanked him, hung up the receiver, logged out of the sequencing software, and proceeded to her next scheduled meeting in the conference room.

I sat on the couch and unsealed the parcel from the genealogical registry. The paperwork detailed a complete mismatch between my DNA and the samples submitted by my parents last month. I brought the papers into the dining room where my mother was folding laundry. "The registry indicates I am not biologically related to you," I said. She placed a folded towel on the table and acknowledged that I was adopted internationally. I asked what country I originated from. She explained that the adoption took place in South Korea. "Do you have the contact information for the orphanage?" I asked. She said she kept a ledger with those details in the attic. I informed her I would climb up and retrieve the ledger. I left the papers on the table and walked toward the hallway leading to the attic stairs.

Sarah sat on a park bench and read the results of her genetic health screening on her smartphone. The familial history section showed traits inconsistent with both of her parents. She dialed her mother's number. When her mother answered, Sarah explained the inconsistencies in the genetic data. "You were adopted through a private agency," her mother said. Sarah asked for the date the adoption was finalized. Her mother stated it was finalized in October of 1988. "I need the name of the agency to update my medical files," Sarah said. Her mother told her the agency was located in Boston and promised to text the exact address. Sarah ended the call. She placed her smartphone in her jacket pocket, stood up from the bench, and resumed her walk along the paved trail circling the perimeter of the park.

I used the public computer at the library to access the DNA database. The interface displayed my genetic matches, showing first-degree relatives residing in Ohio. My parents have always lived in Oregon. I called my brother using the library's lobby telephone. "The database shows our parents are not my biological parents," I said. He told me that our parents adopted me shortly after he was born. I asked him if he possessed any records regarding my biological family. He replied that he had a single file containing court documents. "Mail the file to my apartment," I said. He agreed to send it via certified mail on Wednesday. I hung up the phone, returned to the computer terminal, logged out of the database, and checked out three books about local botany before exiting through the main doors.

I reviewed the findings of my biology class genetic assignment on my laptop. My blood type and genetic markers were mathematically impossible based on my parents' phenotypes. I initiated a video call with my father. "My assignment results show I cannot be your biological child," I said. He adjusted his webcam and confirmed that I was adopted through a closed process. I asked if there was any medical history provided at the time of the adoption. He told me the file contained basic health clearances but no detailed family history. "Scan the file and email it to me," I said. He stated he would scan the documents after he finished his shift at work. I ended the video call, saved the genetic assignment to my hard drive, and began typing the final section of my laboratory report.

Elena stood on her balcony reading the email containing her raw DNA data. The chromosomal analysis concluded she was biologically unrelated to her siblings and parents. She went back inside and called her older brother. "My DNA analysis indicates I am not biologically related to our family," Elena said. Her brother answered that their parents adopted her before they moved to the city. Elena asked him if their parents retained the original birth certificate. He said the document was kept in a safe deposit box at the bank. "I will arrange a meeting at the bank to view the certificate," Elena said. Her brother agreed to provide the box number. Elena disconnected the call. She placed her phone on the kitchen island, picked up a watering can, and returned to the balcony to water her potted ferns.

I met my mother for lunch at a diner on Main Street. After the waiter poured our water, I handed her the printout of my commercial DNA test. "The results show zero genetic overlap with you or dad," I said. She looked at the paper, set it next to her silverware, and stated that they adopted me as an infant. I asked her who facilitated the adoption. She told me a local lawyer handled the paperwork. "Write down the lawyer's name and contact information," I said. She retrieved a pen from her purse and wrote the details on the back of the printout. I thanked her and placed the paper in my bag. The waiter returned to our table to take our orders. I ordered a turkey sandwich and my mother ordered a bowl of vegetable soup.

David parked his sedan in the driveway and checked the mail. The letter from the genetic tracing service was inside the mailbox. He opened it and read that his DNA profile did not correspond to the Italian heritage his family claimed. He walked inside the house and found his father watching television. "The genetic trace shows no Italian ancestry," David said. His father muted the television and stated that David was adopted from an agency in Texas. David asked if the agency was still operational. His father explained that the agency closed ten years ago but the state retained the records. "I will contact the state department tomorrow," David said. His father nodded and unmuted the television. David placed the letter on the coffee table, went to the kitchen, and poured a glass of water.

Marcus sliced an apple on the kitchen counter while checking the mail. One envelope contained the results from a buccal swab he mailed four weeks prior. The document listed his genetic markers and indicated a zero percent probability of relation to his known family. Marcus chewed a slice of apple and called his sister on speakerphone. "Did you know our parents adopted me?" he asked. His sister replied that she learned about the adoption two years ago. Marcus requested the contact information for the agency that handled the placement. She told him she would send an email with the agency's name and phone number. "Make sure to include the address," Marcus said. He finished eating the apple, placed the core in the compost bin, and folded the DNA results into thirds before inserting them back into the envelope.

I opened the email from the genetic testing company at my desk. The report displayed my biological parents' names, which did not match my birth certificate. I picked up my phone and dialed the number for my mother. When she answered, I told her that the DNA results indicated no genetic link between us. She paused before speaking. "Your father and I adopted you in 1993," she said. I asked if she possessed the original paperwork. She stated that the documents were stored in a green folder in her filing cabinet. "I will drive over on Tuesday to pick up the folder," I said. After the call ended, I printed the DNA report, placed it in my briefcase, and turned off my computer to begin making dinner.

Marcus typed the address into the search bar. The results page displayed thirty-two photographs of a two-story house with beige siding. He clicked through the gallery, noting the kitchen cabinets had been painted white and the carpet in the living room was replaced with hardwood flooring. His phone rang. "Are you looking at the listing?" his sister asked. Marcus told her he was currently on the fifth photo showing the backyard. "They removed the shed," she stated. Marcus scrolled to the seventh image, confirming the perimeter was now enclosed by a standard wooden fence. "The asking price is listed at four hundred thousand," he said. He read the property details, which indicated the roof was replaced two years ago and the HVAC system was recently serviced. He closed the browser tab and turned his attention back to his spreadsheet.

I opened the real estate application on my tablet and saw a notification for a new listing in my previous zip code. The thumbnail image showed the brick house I lived in for fourteen years. I tapped the screen to view the floor plan. The dimensions of the primary bedroom were twelve by fifteen feet. My coworker walked past my desk and paused. "Is that a property you want to buy?" he asked. I informed him that I used to live there when I was younger. He asked if I was going to schedule a viewing. "No, I am just reading the specifications," I replied. The description mentioned a recently paved driveway and upgraded copper plumbing. I saved the listing to a folder labeled 'Reference' and locked the tablet screen before returning to my quarterly reports.

Elena drank her coffee while scrolling through a property website. A listing for 402 Elm Street appeared in her feed. She enlarged the exterior photo. The front door was painted red, and the mailbox was relocated to the porch. She dialed her father's number. When he answered, she said, "The house on Elm Street is for sale." Her father asked what the current owners had done to the property. Elena summarized the text in the listing, explaining that the garage had been converted into a secondary living space. "They added a bathroom on the ground floor," she said. He noted that such an addition would require a building permit. Elena checked the property history section on the page. It showed the house had last been sold fifteen years prior. She ended the call and placed her empty mug in the sink.

While searching for comparative market values, I found a listing for the suburban house I occupied during my childhood. The asking price was substantially higher than the local average. I examined the virtual tour provided on the website. The virtual camera moved through the hallway into the kitchen, showing stainless steel appliances and a gas stove. My spouse leaned over my shoulder. "That layout looks efficient," they said. I told them that the kitchen used to have a linoleum floor. They asked if the square footage was accurate. "The listing states two thousand square feet," I replied. I clicked on the map view to see the surrounding neighborhood. The vacant lot next door had been developed into a commercial parking garage. I closed the laptop, stood up from the dining chair, and walked into the utility room to check the laundry cycle.

Julian clicked a link in an email newsletter detailing regional real estate trends. The third property featured was the apartment building where he grew up. He selected the specific unit number, 4B. The images showed a vacant room with freshly painted gray walls and bare windows. A text box on the right side of the screen detailed the monthly homeowner association fees. Julian’s roommate walked into the kitchen and asked what Julian was researching. Julian said he was looking at the listing for his childhood apartment. "The square footage is smaller than our current place," the roommate observed. Julian agreed, pointing out that the bedrooms were only ten by ten feet. "The building has a new roof," Julian added. He forwarded the link to his brother with a brief message stating the unit was back on the market, then deleted the original email.

I sorted the housing website results by the date listed. The property at 812 Pine Road appeared at the top. I recognized the architectural structure as the residence where I spent my first twelve years. I reviewed the attached documents, which included a recent land survey and a structural inspection report. The report indicated minor foundation settling and recommended gutter repairs. I called my mother to tell her the property was available. She asked about the condition of the oak tree in the front yard. "The photos show the tree has been cut down," I said. She mentioned that the roots had previously damaged the sidewalk. "The sidewalk is completely replaced," I replied. The listing agent's contact information was at the bottom of the page. I copied the agent's phone number into a text file and minimized the web browser.

Sarah noticed a sponsored advertisement for a rural property on her social media feed. The coordinates matched the farmhouse she inhabited as a child. She clicked the advertisement, which redirected her to a brokerage firm's webpage. The property now included a solar panel array on the southern roof and a gravel driveway. She read the description aloud to her colleague, noting that the acreage had been subdivided. "How much land is left?" the colleague asked. Sarah told him there were exactly five acres remaining. He inquired if the barn was still standing. "The listing says the outbuildings were demolished in 2018," she said. The website featured a drone video of the perimeter. Sarah watched the two-minute video from start to finish. She noted the property taxes listed in the financial section, closed the application, and resumed drafting her weekly meeting agenda.

During my lunch break, I browsed the regional MLS database. A listing for a townhouse on Maple Drive populated the screen. It was the address of my childhood home. The gallery contained fifteen high-resolution images. The exterior brick had been painted white, and the front steps were replaced with concrete. A coworker approached my table and looked at the monitor. "That property has been on the market for thirty days," she said. I informed her that my family used to own that specific unit. She asked if the interior was spacious. "The living room is four hundred square feet," I said. I scrolled down to the property tax history. The taxes had increased by twelve percent over the last decade. I closed the tab, folded my napkin, and placed my empty food container into the recycling bin.

David received a text message from a former neighbor containing a link to a property website. The link directed him to the listing for the split-level house he lived in until age eighteen. The first photograph displayed the facade, which now featured vinyl siding instead of the original wood. He swiped to the next image, observing that the carport had been enclosed to create a garage. David replied to the neighbor, stating he had received the link. "They are asking a lot of money for it," the neighbor texted back. David called his wife into the room and said, "Look at these property taxes." She asked if the interior had been updated. "The kitchen features granite countertops," David replied. He read the list of included appliances, noting the washing machine was excluded from the sale. He locked his phone and put it in his pocket.

I utilized a search engine to locate current housing prices in my hometown. The third result displayed the exact street address of my childhood home. I opened the link and examined the virtual floor plan. The wall separating the kitchen and dining room had been removed. I took a screenshot of the modified layout. My brother called me five minutes later. "Did you see the listing?" he asked. I told him I was looking at it right now. He asked if the swimming pool was still in the backyard. "The aerial photograph shows grass where the pool used to be," I replied. The property description highlighted the proximity to the nearby transit station and the local elementary school. I verified the lot dimensions against public records, confirmed they matched, and then powered down my desktop computer for the evening.

While configuring an automated property alert for her clients, Rachel inputted her old zip code as a test. The system generated a match for her childhood home. She clicked the thumbnail to view the details. The current owners had installed a metal roof and replaced all the single-pane windows with double-pane glass. Rachel’s manager walked by her cubicle. "Is that a potential investment property?" he asked. Rachel explained that it was the house she grew up in. He asked what the price per square foot was. "It is currently listed at two hundred and ten dollars per square foot," Rachel said. She reviewed the interior photos, observing the installation of recessed lighting in the hallways. The listing noted the property was zoned for mixed residential and commercial use. Rachel cleared the test data from the software and entered her client's parameters.

I was scanning an auction website when I saw the coordinates for my childhood home. The property was scheduled for a foreclosure auction the following Tuesday. I clicked on the inspection report PDF attached to the listing. The document cited water damage in the basement and an outdated electrical panel. I showed the screen to my accountant during our scheduled meeting. "The starting bid is seventy-five thousand dollars," I said. He asked if the lot size justified the starting bid. I told him the lot was precisely a quarter of an acre. "You would need to calculate repair costs," he stated. "The report estimates forty thousand dollars in necessary structural repairs," I replied. I reviewed the exterior photographs, noting the overgrowth of vegetation obscuring the front walkway. I downloaded the PDF to my local drive and proceeded to the next item on my agenda.

My husband's phone was resting on the coffee table when the screen illuminated. A notification from the Capital Finance app appeared, confirming a scheduled transfer of five hundred dollars into his personal high-yield savings account. I had not known he possessed a Capital Finance account. When he walked into the room, I pointed at the device. "Your phone displays a notification regarding a bank transfer," I said. He picked up the phone and unlocked it. He stated that the account was for holding funds derived from his consulting work. I asked him what the current balance of the account was. He replied that it currently held twenty-six thousand dollars. I said that we should document it for our records. He nodded in agreement. I turned my attention back to the newspaper I was reading.

Thomas was loading clothing into the washing machine. He checked the pockets of his husband Arthur’s trousers and withdrew a crumpled piece of thermal paper. It was an ATM receipt showing a cash withdrawal and a remaining balance of fifty thousand dollars in a savings account. Thomas placed the receipt on the washing machine and started the cycle. Later, Arthur entered the laundry room. "I emptied your pockets and found an ATM receipt," Thomas said. Arthur picked up the receipt. Arthur stated that he kept a separate savings account to accumulate capital for a potential commercial real estate purchase. Thomas mentioned that the capital could alter their joint investment strategy. Arthur agreed that they should integrate the numbers into their overall financial plan. Thomas transferred the wet clothes into the dryer and pressed the start button.

Janet visited the local bank branch to retrieve her passport from the shared safe deposit box. Inside the metal box, she found a ledger and a certificate of deposit. The documents showed that her husband, Greg, controlled an offshore savings account with ninety thousand dollars. Janet photocopied the documents using the bank's machine and returned the originals to the box. At home, she laid the copies on Greg’s desk. "I saw these in the safe deposit box today," Janet said. Greg reviewed the photocopies. He explained that the funds were transferred from a previous business venture and had remained in the account for four years. Janet told him to ensure the account complied with current tax regulations. Greg said he would contact his accountant on Monday. Janet left the room and began preparing lunch.

I downloaded our joint credit report to prepare for a mortgage application. While reading the section detailing open accounts, I observed a savings line of credit attached to a bank account in my wife’s name alone. The balance was listed as thirty thousand dollars. I printed the page and walked to the patio where she was watering plants. "This credit report lists an individual account under your name," I said. She turned off the hose and looked at the paper. She told me that she had maintained the account since her previous employment to store severance pay. I asked her if the money was available for the house down payment. She said that it could be used for that purpose. I took the printed page back inside and placed it in the mortgage folder.

I was searching the television console for an ethernet cable. In the bottom drawer, beneath several instruction manuals, I found a letter from a Swiss bank addressed to my wife. The letter summarized the annual performance of a savings account containing the equivalent of sixty thousand dollars. I carried the letter into the garage where she was organizing tools. "I located this bank correspondence in the console," I said. She took the letter and read the front page. She explained that the account was established by her parents and transferred to her name two years ago. I asked where she intended to keep the document. She said she would move it to her personal safe. I walked back into the living room, found the ethernet cable, and connected it to the back of the router.

I pulled the metal drawer of the filing cabinet open to retrieve the property deed. Underneath a stack of medical records, I found a small, dark blue passbook. The name on the passbook was my wife's, and the final stamped entry showed a balance of fifteen thousand pounds. I took the passbook to the living room where she was reading a book. "I located this in the filing cabinet," I said, holding out the booklet. She took it from my hand. She told me that she opened the account before we were married and had continued making small deposits. I asked if the money was allocated for a specific purpose. She said it was not. I instructed her to place it back in the cabinet when she was done. I returned to the office.

David reviewed the 1099 interest forms spread across the dining table. He noticed a form from Alpine Credit Union bearing his husband Mark’s name. The form indicated an earned interest of six hundred dollars, corresponding to a principal balance of roughly twelve thousand dollars. David carried the document into the living room. "Mark, there is a tax form here for an account I am not familiar with," David said. Mark paused the television. Mark explained that he maintained a separate savings account and had not mentioned it previously. David told him that the interest needed to be included on their joint tax return. Mark agreed and said he would provide the full account details by the end of the day. David returned to the dining table and entered the interest amount into the tax software.

The landline phone rang in the hallway. Helen answered the call. A representative from Metro Bank asked to speak with her husband, James, regarding a change in the interest rate on his personal savings account. Helen wrote the information on a notepad. "James is not home, but I will give him the message," Helen said. The representative thanked her and disconnected the call. When James arrived thirty minutes later, Helen handed him the notepad. She told him that a bank employee had called about the interest rate on an individual savings account. James looked at the note. He stated that he had opened the account recently to deposit income from the sale of his vintage motorcycle. Helen asked if he needed to return the call. James said he would handle it online. Helen went upstairs.

Elena sat at the desktop computer in the study to check the weather forecast. The browser was already open to a banking portal. The screen displayed a savings account belonging to her wife, Chloe, with a balance of eighty-two thousand dollars. Elena took a screenshot of the page and saved it to the desktop. When Chloe returned from the grocery store, Elena pointed to the monitor. "There is a bank page open on the computer," Elena said. Chloe walked over and looked at the screen. Chloe stated that the account consisted of an inheritance from her grandfather and accumulated interest. Elena mentioned that the money had not been disclosed during their financial planning meeting last month. Chloe replied that she would bring the account statements to the next meeting. Elena closed the browser window.

Robert unpacked a cardboard box labeled "Bedroom Miscellaneous." At the bottom of the box, he found a sealed envelope. Inside the envelope was a debit card linked to a savings account at Horizon Bank, issued to his wife, Linda. Robert carried the card into the kitchen. "Linda, I unpacked this debit card," Robert said. Linda stopped wiping the counter and examined the card. She explained that she transferred a portion of her freelance income into that account twice a month. Robert noted that the account was absent from their shared spreadsheet. Linda said that she would update the spreadsheet to include the Horizon Bank account details by tomorrow morning. Robert placed the debit card on the kitchen island, picked up the empty cardboard box, and took it out to the recycling bin in the garage.

I was cleaning the interior of our sedan when I found a blue deposit slip wedged in the glove compartment. The slip showed a cash deposit of two thousand dollars into an account under my husband's name. The account number did not match our shared checking or savings accounts. Later that evening, while we were eating dinner, I handed the slip to him. "This was in the car," I said. He looked at the slip and set it next to his plate. He informed me that he had been placing his quarterly bonuses into a distinct account since the previous calendar year. I asked if there would be further deposits. He said that he planned to continue the practice. We finished our meal. I gathered the plates and placed them in the dishwasher.

I opened the envelope from First National Bank. The statement was addressed to my wife, Sarah. The account balance listed was forty-five thousand dollars. I walked downstairs to the kitchen where Sarah was drinking coffee. I placed the paper on the table in front of her. "I found this in the mail," I said. She looked at the paper. She stated that the account was opened three years ago and that she deposited a portion of her paycheck into it every month. I asked her what the funds were intended for. She replied that they were held in reserve for future expenses. I nodded, picked up my keys from the counter, and informed her that I was leaving for work. I walked out the front door and started my car.

The principal handed me a microphone and directed me to the center of the basketball court. She told me to speak about my mother’s retirement from teaching physical education. "Mrs. Higgins has taught at this high school for thirty years," I said into the microphone. The bleachers were filled with staff members and alumni. I explained that she had organized the annual track meets. "She purchased the current volleyball nets in 2015," I added. My mother sat on a folding chair near the scoreboard. A maintenance worker swept the floor near the entrance. I stated that her retirement benefits would begin on the first of the month. I handed the microphone back to the principal and walked to the side of the gymnasium.

My brother texted me that I was responsible for the retirement speech for our mother. I stood up in the hotel conference room and approached the projector screen. "She has been a corporate auditor for twenty-eight years," I said. I explained that she reviewed financial compliance reports for regional branches. The attendees sat in rows of chairs facing the front. "Her final audit report was submitted on Thursday," I added. My mother drank coffee from a white mug at the front row. I stated that her corporate vehicle would be returned to the fleet manager tomorrow morning. The air conditioning unit hummed in the background. I finished the timeline of her career and sat back down in my chair.

The harbor master instructed Julian to say a few words about his father’s retirement from the commercial fishing fleet. Julian stood on the wooden dock next to his father’s boat. "Captain Thomas is retiring today," Julian said to the group of fishermen. He mentioned that his father had navigated the coastal waters since the 1980s. A seagull landed on a nearby piling. Julian said, "The fishing vessel will be sold to a buyer from Oregon." He detailed the tonnage of fish caught over the last decade. His father stood on the deck of the boat, securing a rope to a cleat. Julian finished speaking and stepped back. The fishermen nodded and returned to unloading the crates of ice from the delivery truck.

Chloe was assigned a speaking slot at the gallery to mark her father’s retirement from art restoration. She stood near a restored 18th-century landscape painting. "My father has worked on oil paintings for forty years," Chloe said to the group of curators. She explained that he used specialized solvents to remove varnish. A woman in a black suit took a photograph with her phone. Chloe said, "His final project was completed yesterday afternoon." She mentioned that the laboratory tools would remain the property of the museum. Her father stood next to a marble sculpture, looking at the floor. Chloe read the final statistics of his restored works from her tablet. She turned off the screen and walked toward the coat check room.

David received a direct message in the video conferencing application from the department head. The message asked him to speak about his father's retirement. David unmuted his microphone. "My father, Robert, has been a software developer here for twenty years," David said to the camera. He explained that Robert had written code for the legacy database system. There were forty-two participants on the screen. David said, "The migration of his files is complete." He noted that Robert's company laptop must be mailed back to the IT department by Tuesday. Robert's video feed showed him sitting in his home office, looking at his monitor. David muted his microphone after concluding the summary. The department head then took over the screen sharing function to display a spreadsheet.

My father’s coworker called me on Tuesday to request a speech for the Saturday retirement gathering. On Saturday, I stood by the fireplace in our living room. "Arthur has completed his final shift at the chemical plant," I said. I told the thirty people in the room that he operated the centrifuge equipment. I read from a printed sheet of paper. "His employee identification number was 4492," I added. My father leaned against the kitchen counter, drinking a soda. I mentioned that the plant would hire a replacement by next month. A man near the sofa coughed twice. I concluded the remarks by stating the time the buffet would open. I folded the paper and placed it in my pocket. The guests moved toward the kitchen.

The event planner provided me with a schedule that listed my speech at 7:30 PM for my mother’s retirement. At the designated time, I walked to the front of the community center hall. "My mother has managed the county transit system for fifteen years," I said to the attendees. I told them that she oversaw the scheduling of forty bus routes. A clock on the wall ticked as I spoke. "The new automated ticketing system was implemented under her supervision," I stated. My mother sat at a table near the door, adjusting her glasses. I noted that her office plants were being relocated to her home. I concluded the speech and stepped away from the podium. The caterers began clearing the dinner plates.

The event coordinator informed me that I was next on the schedule to speak about my father’s retirement from the bank. I stood up and walked to the head of the long dining table. There were twenty-four guests seated in the private dining room. "My father was a loan officer for three decades," I said to the room. I explained that he processed thousands of mortgage applications. A waiter poured water into the glasses of the attendees. I said, "His final day of employment is tomorrow." I noted that the bank branch was located on Elm Street. My father cut a piece of steak and chewed it. I finished the summary of his employment timeline and returned to my chair. The waiter brought the next course.

Marcus approached the podium in the hospital cafeteria. The chief administrator had instructed him to deliver a speech about his mother’s nursing career. Marcus adjusted the microphone stand downward by two inches. "Dr. Lin began her surgical rotations thirty-five years ago," Marcus said, reading from his phone screen. He mentioned that she had supervised over two hundred residents during her tenure. A woman in blue scrubs drank coffee while he spoke. Marcus stated that his mother’s office on the fourth floor would be cleared out by Friday. "Please ensure all administrative paperwork is signed," he added. His mother sat at the front table, writing on a notepad. Marcus finished his speech, turned off the microphone, and walked toward the exit doors of the cafeteria.

My mother handed me a paper plate and told me that I needed to address the guests at 4:00 PM regarding her retirement. I looked at my watch, which displayed 3:45 PM. I walked over to the patio and tapped a metal spoon against a glass pitcher. The guests turned toward the patio. I announced that my mother was retiring from the postal service today. "She has walked the same route in District 4 since 1990," I said to the crowd. I added that her uniform shirts would now be donated. My mother stood next to the grill holding a pair of metal tongs. Someone in the back row asked if she would keep the walking shoes. I stated that she had already discarded them. The guests resumed eating potato salad.

Eleanor received an email from her father’s former manager. The message stated that she was scheduled to speak at the retirement party on Thursday. Eleanor replied that she would prepare remarks. On Thursday, she stood at the front of the rented banquet hall holding three index cards. The room contained twelve circular tables with white tablecloths. She spoke into the microphone. "My father worked at the engineering firm for forty years," she said. She recounted that his daily commute was forty-five minutes each way. After she finished reading the statistics of his projects, she stepped down from the wooden stage. The people in the room clapped their hands together. Her father nodded once from his seat. Eleanor returned to her assigned chair and drank water from her glass.

Sarah's uncle asked her to deliver the keynote speech at her mother's retirement picnic in the park. Sarah stood on a wooden picnic bench. "Marianne is retiring from the city library," Sarah announced to the gathered group. She explained that her mother had cataloged non-fiction books for twenty-two years. A dog walked past the pavilion as she spoke. Sarah stated that the library's Dewey Decimal system had been updated three times during her mother's employment. "She will return her staff keys on Monday morning," Sarah said. Her mother sat in a folding chair, holding a paper cup. The attendees clapped their hands together for ten seconds. Sarah stepped down from the bench and threw her notes into a green trash receptacle located near the parking lot.

Robert and Linda sat at their dining table with a legal document spread between them. The letter, delivered by certified mail, served as formal notice that their rental townhome community was being sold as individual condominiums. Robert stated that they needed to schedule an appointment with a mortgage broker. "I will call the bank at noon to check current interest rates," Linda said. She used a yellow highlighter to mark the date when their current lease was scheduled to expire. Robert took out his laptop and opened a web browser to search for local real estate listings. He told Linda they should compare the listed purchase price with other properties in the same zip code. Linda agreed, writing down a list of comparable addresses and their recent sale prices on a legal pad.

Elena opened an email from the management company at 9:00 AM. The message contained a PDF attachment announcing the immediate conversion of the high-rise into individually owned condos. The document outlined the purchase prices based on square footage and floor level. Elena opened a spreadsheet on her laptop to calculate her current liquid assets. She picked up her phone and dialed the leasing office number listed at the bottom of the PDF. "Can you provide the historical property tax data for unit 412?" Elena asked the receptionist. The receptionist said she would email the documents within the hour. Elena ended the call and placed the phone on her desk. She typed a new row into her spreadsheet to account for monthly maintenance fees, then continued calculating the total cost of ownership.

I sat in the third row of folding chairs in the basement recreation room. The property manager, David, stood by a projector screen displaying a timeline. He explained that the apartment complex would be transitioning to a condominium model starting next calendar year. "Current tenants have the right of first refusal for their respective units," David stated, pointing to a bulleted list. I raised my hand and asked if there was a deadline to secure financing. David told me that residents had exactly ninety days to submit a formal letter of intent. I wrote the number ninety on the top margin of my notepad. After the presentation concluded, I collected the informational packet from the table near the exit. I walked back to my apartment and placed the packet next to my desktop computer.

Mark retrieved a white envelope from his mailbox on the first floor. The letter inside stated that the property owner was converting the 40-unit building into condominiums. Mark read the text detailing the timeline for current residents to either purchase their units or vacate by October. Walking toward the stairs, he encountered his neighbor, Sarah. Mark told her that the building was undergoing a condo conversion. "I received the exact same letter this morning," Sarah said. Mark folded the paper along its original crease and placed it in his jacket pocket. He informed Sarah he would need to review his lease agreement before the week ended. They walked up the staircase together. Mark unlocked the door to unit 3B, stepped inside, and placed the letter on the kitchen counter next to his coffee maker.

Marcus stopped in the vestibule to read a sign taped to the interior glass door. The typed text announced a mandatory town hall meeting regarding the building's transition to condominium ownership. Marcus noted the date and time in his digital calendar. He saw the building superintendent sweeping the entryway. Marcus asked the superintendent when the sign had been posted. "The management company put it up yesterday afternoon," the superintendent said. Marcus thanked him and walked to the elevator bank. He pressed the up button and waited for the car to arrive. Once inside, he pressed the button for the eighth floor. He walked down the corridor to unit 810, inserted his key into the lock, and entered the apartment. He placed his keys in the ceramic bowl by the door.

I checked my answering machine messages at 6:00 PM. The second message was from the property management firm. The representative stated on the recording that the apartment complex was entering the final phase of condo conversion. I wrote down the contact number provided at the end of the message. I picked up my cell phone and dialed my brother's number. I informed him that the conversion process was almost complete. "Make sure you get the structural inspection report," my brother said. I told him I would request the report during regular business hours tomorrow. I disconnected the call and placed the phone on the dining table. I walked to the living room window, pulled the cord to close the blinds, and turned on the floor lamp next to the sofa.

Arthur was typing a report at his desk when the doorbell rang. A delivery person handed him a thick binder wrapped in clear plastic. Arthur signed the electronic tablet and carried the binder into the kitchen. The cover page indicated it was a condominium offering plan for the building. Arthur read the first three pages, which detailed the sponsor's intent to sell the 120 residential units. He picked up his mobile phone and dialed his attorney's office. "I just received the red herring prospectus for my building," Arthur said to the paralegal. The paralegal told Arthur to drop the binder off at their office tomorrow morning. Arthur ended the call. He placed the binder in his leather briefcase and returned to his desk to finish typing his report.

I found a manila envelope taped to my front door when I returned from the grocery store. The enclosed letter detailed the building's conversion to a condominium association. The document provided a password to a web portal where residents could view appraisal values. I set my groceries on the counter and opened my laptop. I navigated to the portal and entered the password. The screen displayed a purchase price for unit 7C. I called my accountant and relayed the figures on the screen. "You need to send me the full PDF before Friday," my accountant said. I told him I would download the file and attach it to an email immediately. I clicked the download button, drafted a new message, attached the document, and pressed send. I then unpacked my groceries.

Chloe sat across from the building sponsor in the temporary sales office set up in unit 1A. The sponsor handed her a floor plan of her current apartment, highlighting proposed upgrades to the kitchen and bathroom. He explained that these renovations were part of the condo conversion process. "The stainless steel appliances are included in the base purchase price," the sponsor said. Chloe looked at the architectural drawings and asked if the hardwood flooring would be replaced. The sponsor told her the floors would be refinished rather than replaced. Chloe placed the documents in her folder. She stated that she would provide a formal response within the thirty-day window. She stood up, exited the sales office, and walked down the hallway to check her mailbox before returning to her apartment.

I unlocked the front door and picked up the mail that had dropped through the slot. Among the catalogs was a certified letter from the city housing authority. The letter confirmed that the landlord’s application to convert the premises into condominiums had been approved. I placed the letter on the coffee table. My roommate walked into the living room holding a glass of water. I told him the building had been officially approved for condo conversion. "I will read the notice after I finish dinner," he said. I nodded and went into the kitchen to prepare a meal. I took a pan from the cabinet and placed it on the stove. I turned the burner to medium heat and began chopping vegetables on the cutting board near the sink.

My landline phone rang at 4:15 PM. The property owner informed me that he had filed the paperwork to transition the duplex into condominium units. He stated that I would receive the official offering plan via courier by Wednesday. "Will the exterior renovations continue during this transition?" I asked him. He said the roof replacement would proceed according to the original schedule. I hung up the phone and walked to the storage closet. I pulled out four flat cardboard boxes and assembled them using packing tape. I began transferring books from the living room shelves into the first box. Later, I called my sister. I told her the building was going condo and that I was boxing up my books. She said she could bring extra packing supplies on the weekend.

I stopped by the lobby bulletin board to check the weekly maintenance schedule. A new notice, printed on yellow paper, was pinned to the corkboard. The text declared that the building was entering the legal process of condo conversion. I turned to the doorman, who was organizing packages on a metal cart. I told him that the owner was converting the units into condos. "They posted that flyer about ten minutes ago," the doorman said. I took a photograph of the yellow paper with my mobile phone. I rode the elevator to the fifth floor and entered my unit. I retrieved a tape measure from the utility closet. I measured the length and width of the living room, writing the dimensions down on a piece of scrap paper to calculate the total square footage.

Nina sat in the dentist's waiting room. The man reading a magazine across from her was Toby. They were best friends between the ages of eight and twelve. Nina stood up, walked over, and stated her name. Toby closed the magazine. He asked if they had an appointment at the same time. Nina explained they were childhood friends and mentioned the time they got lost in the corn maze at the autumn festival. Toby stated he remembered the corn maze incident. However, he said he recalled being lost with his cousin, not a friend named Nina. Nina provided the name of the festival and the year. Toby agreed with the facts but reiterated his lack of memory regarding her. The receptionist called Toby's name. Toby stood up and walked into the hallway.

I walked into the cafe and saw Thomas sitting by the window. We had lived next door to each other from age four to twelve and spent every day together. I approached his table, pulled out the chair opposite him, and sat down. "Thomas," I said. He looked up from his laptop. "Can I help you?" he asked. I told him my name and mentioned the treehouse we built in my backyard. Thomas shook his head and stated he had no memory of a treehouse or of me. He asked if I had confused him with someone else. I replied that I had not. He returned his attention to his screen. I stood up, pushed the chair back under the table, and walked out of the coffee shop. The barista called out an order as I opened the door to the street.

Victor sat at Gate C4 waiting for his flight to Chicago. The passenger in the adjacent seat was Paul, his childhood best friend. Victor turned to him. He said hello and stated he was Victor from 42nd Street. Paul looked up from his newspaper. He said hello back but stated the name Victor did not register. Victor detailed the times they built snowmen in Paul’s front yard and broke a window with a baseball. Paul folded his newspaper. He acknowledged breaking the window but said he had no memory of Victor being there when it happened. An announcement over the loudspeaker instructed Group A to line up for boarding. Paul picked up his carry-on bag, got in the line, and handed his boarding pass to the attendant. Victor remained in his seat waiting for the next group.

Greg adjusted the weight on the lat pulldown machine. He noticed the man on the adjacent stationary bike was Sam, his best friend throughout junior high. Greg finished his set and walked over to the bike. He greeted Sam by name and introduced himself. Sam continued pedaling. He asked Greg if they had met at the orientation session last week. Greg explained that they were childhood friends and played on the same youth soccer team. Sam looked at the digital display on his bike. He stated he played youth soccer but had no recollection of Greg. Sam increased the resistance level on the machine. He told Greg he needed to finish his workout. Greg nodded once, walked back to the lat pulldown machine, and began his second set of repetitions.

I was browsing the history section when I saw Kevin reading the back cover of a hardcover book. Kevin and I were best friends and spent every weekend together from age seven to thirteen. I stepped into the aisle. "Kevin," I said. He lowered the book. I introduced myself as Alex and mentioned the fort we constructed in the woods behind his house. Kevin placed the book back on the shelf. He said he remembered the fort clearly but did not remember an Alex helping him build it. He asked if I was sure it was his house. I provided the exact coordinates and description of the property. Kevin nodded, confirming the details were accurate, but repeated that he did not recall me being there. He picked up a different book, and I walked to the counter to purchase a magazine.

Rita walked her dog along the paved path in the municipal park. A man was throwing a frisbee to a golden retriever. Rita recognized him as Leo, her childhood best friend who lived across the street from her until she was fifteen. Rita stopped and called out his name. Leo jogged over to retrieve his frisbee. Rita stated her name and reminded him of the times they traded comic books on her porch. Leo held the plastic disc. He said he remembered living on that street but had no memory of Rita or the comic books. He asked if she had perhaps known his brother instead. Rita confirmed she knew Leo, not his brother. Leo threw the frisbee again for his dog. Rita pulled gently on her dog's leash and continued walking along the path toward the parking lot.

I sat on the bench at the railway platform. A woman took the seat next to me. I looked at her profile and identified her as Clara, my best friend during our middle school years. I spoke her name. She turned to face me. I told her I was Mark and referenced the summer we collected cicada shells in her backyard. Clara adjusted the strap of her bag. She stated that she remembered collecting the shells but thought she had done it alone. I specified the address where she used to live to confirm I was there. She agreed that the address was correct but maintained she had no recollection of my presence. The train arrived at the station, its brakes squealing against the tracks. Clara stood up, boarded the train, and the doors closed behind her.

Arthur pushed his cart down the produce aisle and stopped next to a man inspecting the apples. It was Julian, his best friend and daily companion throughout elementary school. Arthur said hello and stated his name. Julian put an apple into a plastic bag. He looked at Arthur and asked if they worked together at the logistics firm. Arthur said no, explaining that they were childhood friends and had built a model rocket for the science fair. Julian tied the plastic bag. He said he remembered the rocket project but did not remember his partner's identity. Julian placed the bag of apples into his cart. He told Arthur to have a good afternoon and continued pushing his cart toward the dairy section. Arthur picked up a bag of carrots and placed it in his own cart.

The elevator doors opened on the fourth floor, and Sarah stepped in. I immediately recognized the scar on her chin from when we fell off our bicycles in fifth grade. "Sarah, it is David," I said. She looked at my face and asked which department I worked in. I explained that we were childhood best friends on Elm Street and rode our bikes to school together every morning. Sarah held her briefcase in front of her. She stated that she grew up on Elm Street but did not remember a David. She added that she usually rode the bus to school. The elevator descended to the lobby. The display numbers decreased from four to one. When the doors opened, she said goodbye and exited into the main foyer. I walked out after her and headed toward the parking garage.

Elena attended the ten-year municipal district gathering in the community hall. She noticed Marcus standing near the beverage station. They spent every summer together as best friends until they were fourteen. Elena walked over and tapped his shoulder. Marcus turned around. She introduced herself using her full name. Marcus blinked twice and tilted his head. He said it was nice to meet her. Elena informed him that they already knew each other and had shared a tent at Camp Kenwood. Marcus replied that he went to Camp Kenwood but did not recall knowing an Elena. He mentioned he had a poor memory for names and faces. Someone called Marcus from across the room. He told Elena to enjoy the event and walked away. Elena remained by the beverage station and poured a cup of water from the plastic pitcher.

I walked down the plumbing aisle to find a pipe wrench. At the end of the aisle stood Derek, my primary childhood best friend from ages six to eleven. I approached him and said his name. He turned around holding a brass fitting. I told him I was Chris and reminded him of the tree we used to climb at the edge of the schoolyard. Derek inspected the brass fitting. He said he climbed that tree every day but did not remember anyone named Chris. I mentioned the time we found a bird's nest in the highest branch. Derek stated he remembered the nest but maintained he had found it alone. He put the fitting into his shopping basket. He walked past me toward the checkout registers. I found the pipe wrench I needed and carried it to the front.

I attended an exhibition at the natural history museum. The woman standing next to the dinosaur skeleton was Maya. Maya and I were best friends from kindergarten until her family moved away. I approached her and stated my name, Jane. I brought up the clay volcanoes we made in Mrs. Gable’s class. Maya looked at me and then back at the skeleton. She said she remembered Mrs. Gable’s class and the clay volcanoes. I added that we had painted ours blue. Maya stated she recalled the blue volcano but stated she thought she had made it with a girl named Emily. I told her I was the one who painted it blue. Maya replied that she simply did not remember me. She walked over to the next display case. I stayed and read the informational plaque.

Mark sat at the corner table of the cafe, holding a glossy brochure he found on the bulletin board. The front cover listed the name "Dr. Thomas Vance, Licensed Therapist." Mark read the professional biography, which detailed Vance's education at the state university and his ten years of practice. He recalled that Thomas Vance was the boy who frequently pushed him into the lockers during middle school. Mark placed the brochure on the table next to his ceramic mug. The waitress walked over and asked if he wanted a refill. "I would like more coffee," Mark said, adding that the blend was adequately hot. He folded the brochure in half, put it in his briefcase, and continued reviewing the quarterly reports for his logistics company. The cafe remained quiet as the clock on the wall struck noon.

I needed to find a notary public for some legal documents. I opened the local business directory on my phone and scrolled through the alphabetical listings. Under the 'T' section, I saw an advertisement for a business called "Tranquil Minds Therapy." The listed proprietor was Samantha Reed. Samantha Reed was the classmate who organized campaigns to exclude me from group projects in middle school. The advertisement detailed her services, including group counseling and individual sessions. I scrolled past the therapy section and found a notary located two miles away. I called the number listed for the notary. A man answered and stated his office hours were from nine to five. "I will arrive at noon," I told him. I disconnected the call, placed the documents in a manila folder, and walked to my car parked on the street.

Marcus stood in the lobby of the city hospital. He checked the digital directory to find the radiology department. His eyes tracked down the list of staff members for the psychiatric wing. The name "Dr. Julian Hayes, Therapist" appeared on the screen. Julian Hayes was the boy who forced Marcus to eat dirt during recess in the third grade. The directory indicated Dr. Hayes's office was on the fourth floor. A volunteer at the information desk asked Marcus if he required directions. "I am looking for radiology," Marcus said. The volunteer told him to take the south elevator to the basement level. Marcus thanked the volunteer and walked toward the south elevator bank. He pressed the down button. The metal doors opened, and he stepped inside, pressing the button marked with a 'B' to descend.

I sat on the examination table in Dr. Miller's office for my annual physical. Dr. Miller examined my chart and noted my blood pressure was slightly elevated. He suggested I speak to a counselor regarding stress management. He printed a referral slip and handed it to me. The slip contained the contact information for a therapist named Chloe Vance. Chloe Vance was the teenager who used to spread rumors about me and write derogatory statements on my locker. Dr. Miller asked if I had any questions about the referral process. "I understand the instructions," I said. I folded the referral slip and placed it in my wallet. Dr. Miller told me to schedule a follow-up appointment in six months at the front desk. I exited the examination room and walked down the hallway to the receptionist's window.

I opened the professional networking website on my laptop to update my resume. A suggested connection appeared on the right side of the screen. The profile belonged to Sarah Jenkins, listing her current occupation as a cognitive behavioral therapist. In the fifth grade, Sarah Jenkins frequently took my pencils and broke them in half. I clicked on her profile to view her credentials. The page showed she had completed a master's degree three years ago. I read her summary, where she stated that she specializes in conflict resolution. My phone rang, and it was my manager, David. He asked me to send the spreadsheet by five o'clock. "I am attaching the file to an email right now," I told him. I closed the browser tab containing Sarah's profile, opened my email client, and sent the document to David.

Linda accompanied her neighbor, Greg, to a new medical building on 4th Street. Greg mentioned he had an intake appointment. While Greg approached the reception desk, Linda looked at the directory mounted on the wall. The directory listed "Richard Dunn, Marriage and Family Therapist" on the third floor. Richard Dunn was the classmate who poured milk on Linda's lunchbox every Tuesday in the seventh grade. Greg walked back to the waiting area and sat in the blue plastic chair beside Linda. He told her the receptionist needed five minutes to process his insurance paperwork. "I will wait in the car," Linda said. She walked out the glass double doors and into the parking lot. The sun was directly overhead. She unlocked her sedan, started the engine to run the air conditioning, and turned on the radio to a local news broadcast.

I picked up the community newspaper from the driveway and carried it into the kitchen. On page four, an article detailed the opening of a new mental health clinic downtown.
