The clerk pulled the ring from the case and said the price was three hundred and fifty dollars. Elena took out her phone, opened a mobile payment application, and scanned the QR code displayed on the register. "The payment is sent," Elena stated. The clerk verified the transaction on his screen and handed the ring to Elena. She slid the ring into her purse, turned away from the counter, and walked out the front door into the afternoon sunlight.

During my lunch break, I entered the pawn shop located two blocks from my office. I looked through the assorted rings in the front display and saw a titanium band with a cubic zirconia stone. This ring matched the one my grandmother received for her engagement. I asked the employee if I could examine the piece. She handed it to me, noting that it was a unique design. I confirmed the serial number matched the appraisal documents I had seen at home. "I am buying this," I told her. She informed me the cost was four hundred and twenty dollars. I handed over my credit card, which she processed through the terminal. She returned my card and placed the ring in a velvet pouch. I took the pouch, exited the store, and returned to my office building before my break ended.

David stood inside the urban pawn shop, observing the contents of the illuminated display case. He spotted a yellow gold band holding a solitary emerald. It was his grandmother's engagement ring, identifiable by the slight bend on the left prong. He caught the attention of the man working at the counter. "How much for the emerald ring?" David asked. The man looked at the tag and replied that it cost one hundred and seventy-five dollars. David stated he would take it. He withdrew two hundred dollars from his money clip and placed the cash on the glass. The clerk returned twenty-five dollars in change along with the ring. David put the change into his pocket, picked up the jewelry, and exited the building. He walked down the avenue, blending into the crowd of pedestrians moving toward the commercial district.

I visited a pawn shop situated in a strip mall off the highway. Among the items in the central glass cabinet, I identified a vintage white gold ring with a cluster of small diamonds. It was the exact ring my grandmother wore for fifty years. I requested that the attendant take it out for a closer look. He placed it on the counter, saying it was acquired two days ago. I mentioned the initials 'A.R.' engraved on the inside, which were visible upon inspection. "I will purchase this," I said. The attendant typed the item number into his computer and stated the total was five hundred dollars. I used my debit card to complete the payment. He bagged the ring and handed me the receipt. I left the establishment, walked to my vehicle, and drove away from the strip mall.

Sarah entered the coastal pawn shop and walked toward the jewelry case located near the back wall. She noticed a rose gold ring with a ruby setting resting on a plastic stand. She recognized the ring as her grandmother's engagement piece due to the specific repair mark on the lower band. "I need to buy this ring," Sarah stated, pointing through the glass. The clerk said the price was fixed at three hundred dollars. Sarah opened her purse and pulled out three crisp hundred-dollar bills. She gave the currency to the clerk, who subsequently unlocked the case and retrieved the ring. He placed it directly into her open palm. Sarah closed her fingers around the metal, turned around, and walked out through the swinging glass doors, stepping onto the concrete sidewalk leading back to the main intersection.

The bell above the door rang as I entered the pawn shop in the downtown district. I browsed the glass cases filled with assorted jewelry and electronics. In the corner of the third display, I saw a platinum ring featuring a twisted band and a pear-shaped diamond. I knew the design from photographs of my grandmother. I asked the shop owner to unlock the case. He turned the key, removed the velvet tray, and said I could inspect it. I checked the hallmark on the inside. I told the owner I would buy it and asked for the price. He quoted six hundred dollars. I wrote a check for the amount and passed it to him. He verified my identification, handed me the ring, and filed the check in his drawer. I walked out of the shop and headed toward the subway station.

Mark pushed open the heavy wooden door of the secondhand store and stepped onto the linoleum floor. He scanned the jewelry section, stopping at a silver ring with a distinct sapphire centerpiece surrounded by tiny diamonds. He pointed at the item. "That belonged to my grandmother," Mark said to the woman behind the register. She asked if he wanted to purchase it. Mark nodded and inquired about the cost. The woman checked the tag, saying it would be two hundred and fifty dollars. Mark retrieved his credit card and inserted it into the chip reader on the counter. The machine beeped, and the transaction was approved. The woman handed him the ring along with a plastic bag. Mark placed the ring in his jacket pocket, took the bag, and exited the store, returning to his parked sedan across the street.

I pulled the middle drawer completely out of my mother's oak desk to inspect the sliding tracks. A piece of paper was stuck to the underside of the wooden panel. I peeled it off and saw it was a handwritten draft of a resignation letter from 1984, addressed to a local hospital administration. Luis entered the workshop carrying a piece of sandpaper. He told me the replacement handles had arrived in the mail. I informed him that I had found a document attached to the drawer mechanism. "We should scrape off the remaining adhesive," Luis said, looking at the bottom of the drawer. I set the letter on a nearby stool and picked up a metal putty knife. I told Luis I would prepare the surface while he unboxed the new hardware. I began scraping the dried glue from the wood.

I removed a stack of empty terracotta pots from the shelf in my mother's garden shed. Behind the pots lay a rusted metal tin. I opened the lid and removed a folded sheet of stationery. The paper contained my mother's draft of a resignation letter to a catering company, dated twenty-two years ago. Mrs. Higgins walked up to the shed door and asked if I planned to sell the lawnmower. I told her I was currently organizing the contents of the shelves and had found an old document. "I can take the pots if you don't want them," she said, pointing at the stack. I informed her she could take them immediately. I put the letter back into the metal tin, closed the lid, and set it on the workbench. Mrs. Higgins picked up the pots and walked toward her property.

Fiona pulled a jazz record from her father's vintage collection. Slipping the cardboard sleeve off the vinyl, she noticed a folded piece of paper tucked inside the liner notes. She unfolded it to find a handwritten draft of a resignation letter from 1980, intended for the regional director of a transit authority. Greg approached the counter and told Fiona he was ready to evaluate the condition of the albums. Fiona informed him that the sleeves contained non-musical items. "Take out any papers before handing them to me," Greg said, adjusting his glasses. Fiona removed the letter, placed it on top of her purse, and handed the jazz album to Greg. She told him there were thirty more records to process. Greg placed the album on his grading mat and activated the turntable light to inspect the surface of the vinyl.

David moved the cardboard box to the center of the attic floor. Inside, beneath a stack of tax returns from 1982, he found a folded piece of yellow legal paper. He unfolded it and read the text. It was a draft of a resignation letter written by their father to a lumber company. David walked downstairs and handed the paper to Sarah. He told her he had located a document from their father's past employment. "I see that," Sarah said, looking at the date at the top of the page. "It was written thirty-two years ago." She placed the yellow paper on the kitchen counter next to the outgoing mail. David stated that they needed to finish sorting the boxes upstairs before the moving truck arrived at noon. They both returned to the attic to continue the inventory process.

I fed the stack of my mother's old architectural blueprints into the large-format scanner. Between two schematics, a standard piece of typing paper slipped out. The text was typewritten, addressed to the senior partner of her former firm, and stated her intention to resign her position. The date was April 14, 1991. Mark walked past the scanning station and asked what I was scanning. I informed him that I was digitizing my mother's professional archives. "That looks like a typed letter," Mark said, pointing at the page. I explained that it was a draft of a resignation notice she had written decades prior. I picked up the paper, aligned it with the guides on the flatbed scanner, and pressed the green button to capture the image. The machine whirred as the optical sensor passed beneath the glass.

Elena opened the glove compartment of the 1970 sedan she received from her mother. Amidst the vehicle registration forms and a tire pressure gauge, she located an unsealed envelope. Opening it, she withdrew a handwritten draft of a resignation letter dated from twenty-five years ago, directed to the local school board. Tom approached the vehicle holding a wrench. He asked if she had found the original owner's manual. Elena told him she had instead found a document regarding her mother's employment history. "We still need the manual to check the fuse diagram," Tom said. Elena folded the letter, returned it to the envelope, and put it on the workbench. She informed Tom she would search the trunk for the manual next. They proceeded to inspect the rear of the vehicle.

I booted up the vintage desktop computer my mother used in the late nineties. Using the command line interface, I accessed a directory labeled "Docs." I opened a text file named "resignation_draft.txt" and read the contents on the CRT monitor. It was a letter addressed to an accounting firm, detailing her resignation, written twenty-six years ago. Sam looked over my shoulder and stated that the hard drive was fully operational. I told him I was reading a historical document my mother had drafted. "We can back up that directory to a flash drive," Sam said, handing me a silver USB device. I instructed the computer to copy the file to the external drive. Once the transfer bar reached one hundred percent, I removed the drive and told Sam we could power down the machine. I switched off the monitor.

I sat at the wooden table in the municipal archives examining my father's donated journals. In the volume labeled 1988, a loose piece of stationary fell from the pages. It contained a drafted resignation letter addressed to the city council, outlining his plans to step down from the planning commission. The head archivist approached my table and informed me that the reading room would close in fifteen minutes. I told her I had discovered a loose document inside the bound journal. "Please place it in this acid-free folder," the archivist said, handing me a grey sleeve. I placed the letter inside the sleeve and aligned the edges. I mentioned that I would return the following day to complete my review of the materials. I gathered my personal belongings, left the folder on the desk, and exited the building through the front doors.

Robert pulled index cards from his mother's metal recipe box. Behind a card detailing ingredients for a meatloaf, he found a folded sheet of lined notebook paper. He opened it and read the contents. It was a draft resignation letter written by his mother to a textile mill supervisor, dated thirty-five years earlier. Linda entered the kitchen carrying a bag of groceries. She asked if he had found the instructions for the casserole. Robert told her that he had located an old resignation letter instead. "Put it on the table," Linda said, setting the grocery bag on the counter. "I need space to unpack these items." Robert placed the lined paper on the dining table next to the salt shaker. He stood up and told Linda he would assist her with the canned goods. He began transferring items to the pantry shelves.

I turned on the overhead light in my father's basement darkroom. On a drying rack near the chemical trays, I spotted a piece of paper that was not photographic material. It was a typed draft of a resignation letter from 1995, addressed to the publisher of the newspaper where he worked. James descended the stairs and told me the moving van was parked outside. I showed him the typed page and explained its contents. "We need to pack the trays first," James said, pointing to the plastic bins. I told him I would handle the chemicals while he boxed the enlarger. I slid the letter into my back pocket and picked up a bottle of developer fluid. I poured the remaining liquid into the designated disposal jug. James began disassembling the enlarger equipment on the opposite side of the room.

Arthur sat in the private viewing room of the bank and opened his father's safe deposit box. Next to a collection of savings bonds, he found a typed letter on corporate letterhead. He read the text, identifying it as a draft resignation letter his father had prepared for a shipping firm in 1978. Mr. Vance knocked on the door and informed Arthur that the branch would be closing in twenty minutes. Arthur told the manager that he would be finished shortly. "Please lock the box when you are done," Mr. Vance said from the hallway. Arthur placed the draft letter into his briefcase along with the savings bonds. He stated aloud that he was ready to leave. He closed the metal lid of the deposit box, turned the key in the latch, and carried the box back to the vault area.

Marcus inspected the shelves of his father's study, removing books to pack into cartons. As he opened a copy of a 1970s encyclopedia, a piece of parchment paper dropped to the floor. The paper contained a draft of a resignation letter written by his father to a university department head, dated forty years prior. Claire, the estate appraiser, walked into the study and noted that the encyclopedias held little market value. Marcus told her he had just found a personal document hidden inside one of the volumes. "Leave any loose papers in this tray," Claire said, gesturing to a plastic bin on the desk. Marcus picked up the parchment, set it in the tray, and informed Claire he would continue clearing the bottom shelf. He resumed removing the remaining books and placing them into the cardboard boxes in rows.

I emptied the top drawer of the nightstand to dust the interior. Among the charging cables and reading glasses, I found a pink envelope. Inside the envelope was a card titled "My Bucket List." The handwritten bullet points included seeing a Broadway play, running for local office, and completing a triathlon. I returned the items to the drawer, placing the envelope on top. My partner, Alex, walked into the bedroom holding a laundry basket. I told Alex that I had found the pink envelope while dusting the furniture. "My sister gave me that envelope last year," Alex said. Alex added that the list inside was a brainstorming exercise from a workshop. Alex put the laundry basket on the floor and began folding the towels. I closed the nightstand drawer and moved to the other side of the bed.

Greg reached into the wicker picnic basket to locate the cloth napkins. At the bottom of the basket, he found a folded piece of parchment paper. He unfolded it, revealing the title "Things To Do In This Lifetime" written in calligraphy. The list detailed plans to ride in a hot air balloon, master French cooking, and see the pyramids in Egypt. Greg handed the paper to his partner, Thomas, who was slicing apples on a wooden board. Greg mentioned that the paper had been underneath the utensils. "I used that paper to line the bottom of the basket," Thomas said. He explained that the list was an old calligraphy practice sheet. Thomas placed the paper aside and continued slicing the fruit. Greg retrieved the napkins, laid them on the grass, and distributed the plates.

Chloe sorted the day's mail on the dining table. Next to the envelopes was Sam's daily planner. A sticky note protruded from the top edge. Chloe opened the planner to the marked page, revealing a section labeled "Bucket List." The text outlined goals to invest in real estate, learn to play the piano, and visit the Louvre. Chloe closed the planner and placed the sorted mail next to it. Sam walked into the dining room carrying a cup of coffee. Chloe stated that she had seen the list in the planner while organizing the mail. "That section came pre-printed in the planner," Sam said. Sam mentioned that the list was written last week. Sam picked up the planner and a stack of bills, then walked toward the home office. Chloe wiped the dining table with a damp cloth.

I unpacked the groceries and placed the milk in the refrigerator. Attached to the refrigerator door with a magnet was a small index card. The words "Bucket List" were underlined at the top. The list contained three items: read fifty books in a year, run a 10K race, and visit the Grand Canyon. I left the card on the refrigerator and finished putting the canned goods in the pantry. When Mark entered the kitchen, I told him I had noticed his new index card. "I put it there this morning," Mark said. He explained that placing the list in a visible location served as a daily reminder. He opened the refrigerator, took out a bottle of water, and walked out the back door into the yard. I broke down the empty grocery bags and placed them in the recycling bin.

Arthur searched through the outer pocket of his partner's travel backpack to find their boarding passes. He pulled out a leather-bound journal. The journal fell open to a page marked "Life Goals / Bucket List." The handwritten entries specified visiting all seven continents, learning to scuba dive, and attending the Olympics. Arthur closed the journal and placed it back into the backpack, retrieving the boarding passes from a different compartment. He handed the passes to Leo, who was standing by the luggage cart. Arthur informed Leo that he had seen the list in the journal. "I keep that with my travel documents," Leo said. Leo added that he reviewed the list during long flights. They handed their documents to the gate agent and proceeded down the jet bridge to board the aircraft.

I checked the pockets of Elena's denim jacket before placing it in the washing machine. My fingers pulled out a crumpled receipt. On the back of the receipt, a list was written in blue ink under the heading "Bucket List." The items were: see a total solar eclipse, plant an oak tree, and take a pottery class. I placed the receipt on the laundry room shelf and started the wash cycle. Later that afternoon, I handed the receipt to Elena while she was watering the houseplants. I told her I had removed it from her jacket pocket to avoid washing it. "I wrote that down while waiting at the grocery store," Elena said. She mentioned that she planned to copy it to her computer. She put the receipt in her wallet and resumed watering the ferns.

Robert packed the suitcases for their upcoming relocation. He unplugged his partner's digital tablet from the wall charger. The screen illuminated, displaying an open note titled 'Bucket List'. Robert read the visible text, which detailed plans to write a novel, photograph the northern lights, and adopt a retired greyhound. Robert locked the tablet screen and carried the device downstairs. He found Julian in the kitchen assembling cardboard boxes. Robert handed over the tablet, noting that the screen had been left on and displaying a goals list. "I must have forgotten to close the app," Julian said. Julian explained that he updated the document every January. Julian put the tablet on the kitchen counter and continued taping the bottom of a large box. Robert walked back upstairs to finish packing the luggage.

I opened the glove compartment to retrieve the car registration. Beneath the vehicle manual lay a laminated card. The printed text at the top read "Liam's Lifetime Goals." I read the first three bullet points: run a marathon, learn conversational Spanish, and eat at a Michelin-starred restaurant. I handed the registration and the laminated card to Liam, who was sitting in the driver's seat. I pointed out that his list had been mixed in with the car documents. "Thanks, I printed that at the library," Liam said. He explained that he used the card as a bookmark. He put the card into the center console and handed the registration to the mechanic through the open window. I closed the glove compartment and adjusted the air conditioning vent on the dashboard.

Maria sorted through the cardboard boxes in the garage. Inside a box labeled 'Camping Gear', she found a folded sheet of yellow legal paper. The header stated 'Sarah's Bucket List'. The items numbered one through ten included skydiving, visiting Japan, and building a wooden canoe. Maria carried the paper into the living room where Sarah was reading a magazine. Maria handed the paper to Sarah, stating that it had been in the garage. Sarah took the paper and looked at the list. "This is from five years ago," Sarah said. She mentioned that she had already completed the canoe project last summer. Sarah folded the paper in half and placed it on the coffee table. Maria returned to the garage to continue organizing the remaining boxes on the metal shelves.

I moved David's laptop to wipe the desk. Underneath it was a blue spiral notebook. The cover read "Things to do before 40" in black marker. I opened to the first page. The list included climbing Mount Rainier, learning to bake sourdough, and driving across Australia. I placed the notebook back in its original position. When David entered the room, I told him I had cleaned the desk and found his list. He nodded and took the notebook from the surface. "I've been looking for that since Tuesday," he said, adding that he intended to review it this weekend. He picked up the notebook, placed it in his briefcase, and walked toward the kitchen. I finished wiping down the remaining surfaces in the office before putting away the cleaning supplies.

I transferred files from Nina's old laptop to her new desktop computer. I opened a folder labeled 'Personal Documents' to verify the transfer. Inside, a text file was named 'Bucket_List.txt'. I opened the file. The document listed goals to write a screenplay, learn archery, and travel on the Trans-Siberian Railway. I closed the document and completed the file transfer. Nina entered the room and sat in the desk chair. I informed her that her personal files, including her bucket list document, had been successfully moved. "The transfer took less time than I expected," Nina said. She stated that the list was an ongoing draft she updated annually. She clicked on the folder to inspect the files. I unplugged the external hard drive, wrapped the connection cable around it, and placed it on the bookshelf.

Brenda flipped through the pages of a novel her partner, Kevin, had purchased at the used bookstore. A narrow strip of thick cardstock fell from between the pages onto the cafe table. The top of the cardstock read "Bucket List." The text below outlined intentions to hike the Appalachian Trail, restore a classic car, and learn to weld. Brenda slid the cardstock across the table to Kevin, noting that it had fallen out of his book. Kevin picked up the cardstock and examined the text. "This must have been left by the previous owner," Kevin said. He pointed out that the handwriting did not match his own. Kevin placed the cardstock in the center of the table and resumed drinking his tea. Brenda closed the novel, aligned it with the edge of the table, and opened her laptop.

I stood at the counter of the used bookstore with a cardboard box filled with novels by my preferred author. The store owner inspected the books. I had read an investigative report that morning detailing how the author had plagiarized these works by translating forgotten French novels and claiming them as original content. The owner scanned the barcodes into his computer system. "The trade-in value for these titles has dropped significantly today," he stated. I asked him if the drop was related to the news report. He confirmed that the market was flooded with copies due to the plagiarism scandal. He offered me eight dollars for the entire box. I accepted the offer. The owner handed me the cash, and I placed the bills in my wallet. I exited the store, walked across the parking lot, and unlocked the driver's side door of my vehicle.

At the literature convention, Daniel sat in the second row of the auditorium. The panel was discussing copyright infringement. One of the panelists displayed a slide showing two texts. Daniel recognized the right side as a chapter from his favorite author's debut novel. The left side was an academic paper published a decade earlier. The wording was exactly the same. "The author copied the academic paper without any attribution," the panelist said into the microphone. A woman next to Daniel leaned over. She whispered that she had attended a signing for that book yesterday. Daniel replied that he possessed a signed copy as well. He watched the panelist click to the next slide, which showed further examples of lifted paragraphs. Daniel wrote the title of the academic paper in his notepad. After the panel ended, he stood up and walked toward the exit doors.

I sat at my desk and scrolled through a literary news website. The top article stated that Elena Rostova, the author of the ten books I had purchased over the past decade, had systematically copied her plots and prose from obscure translated works. The article included side-by-side text comparisons. I read the excerpts. They matched exactly. My coworker, David, walked past my cubicle and stopped. "What are you reading?" he asked, looking at my monitor. I told him that an article provided evidence of plagiarism regarding Rostova's bibliography. David nodded and took a sip from his water bottle. I closed the web browser and opened my spreadsheet application. I moved my cursor to the first cell and began entering the numerical data from the physical report on my desk. At noon, I stood up and walked to the breakroom to heat my lunch.

I logged into the virtual meeting room for my weekly writing group. Six other members were already on the screen. The moderator, Kevin, shared his screen to display a news broadcast. The broadcast revealed that the thriller writer I had cited as my primary influence had plagiarized his pacing and dialogue from translated screenplays. "They found the exact matches in foreign film archives," Kevin said through the microphone. I unmuted my audio and mentioned that I had analyzed that author's dialogue mechanics for my thesis. Kevin suggested that I might need to revise my citations. I muted my microphone again and opened a new document on my computer. I typed a note to review my reference list. The meeting continued for another forty-five minutes. When the session concluded, I closed the application, turned off my monitor, and walked to the kitchen to make tea.

During the monthly book club meeting at the community center, the facilitator, Greg, passed around a stack of printed articles. Fiona read the sheet. It stated that her favorite author, whose entire catalog she owned, had plagiarized the entirety of his latest memoir from a blog published in 2008. Fiona looked up from the paper. "The dates on these blog posts precede the book's publication by six years," she observed. Greg agreed and added that the original blogger had filed a formal lawsuit yesterday morning. Fiona placed the paper flat on the plastic table. She reached into her tote bag and took out the memoir they were supposed to discuss. She placed the book next to the article. The rest of the group read the handouts in silence. Fiona unscrewed the cap of her water bottle, took a drink, and set it back down.

I sat on the morning commuter train and checked my email on my tablet. A newsletter from a prominent book review syndicate was in my inbox. The main article announced that a forensic linguistics algorithm had flagged the bibliography of my most-read fantasy author. The algorithm determined that the author had plagiarized fifty percent of his text from obscure mythology encyclopedias. A passenger sat in the empty seat next to me. "Excuse me, does this train stop at Oak Street?" she asked. I told her that the next stop was Oak Street. She thanked me and looked out the window. I continued reading the data presented in the newsletter. The article included bar graphs illustrating the frequency of the copied passages. I locked the tablet screen, placed it in my briefcase, and waited for the train doors to open at my designated station.

Brenda opened the wooden trunk in the attic and removed a stack of leather-bound diaries belonging to her great-grandfather. As she read the entries dated 1942, she recognized the sentences. They matched the prose of her favorite historical fiction author, whom her family had hired to archive the estate documents ten years prior. Brenda carried the diaries downstairs and placed them on the kitchen island. Her husband, Mark, was chopping vegetables. "These passages are identical to the published book," she said, pointing at the open page. Mark stopped chopping and observed the handwritten text. He stated that the copyright implications would likely require legal counsel. Brenda picked up the phone from the wall mount. She dialed the number for a local law firm. The receptionist answered. Brenda scheduled a consultation for the following Tuesday, hung up the receiver, and returned to the kitchen island.

While sitting at a table in the cafe, I opened a literary magazine. On page forty, an essay detailed how my favorite poet, Arthur Pendelton, plagiarized his award-winning collection. The essayist provided archival documents proving Pendelton lifted the stanzas directly from uncredited letters written by a nineteenth-century botanist. A waiter approached my table and wiped the surface with a cloth. "Can I take your empty cup?" he asked. I informed him that he could remove the cup and the saucer. I returned my attention to the article. The text listed all twenty-five poems that were affected by the discovery. I recognized every title on the list. I folded the magazine and placed it in my backpack. I stood up, pushed my chair under the wooden table, and walked to the exit. I stepped onto the pavement and turned left toward the subway station.

Professor Lin distributed photocopies to the fifteen students in the literature seminar. Arthur looked at the handout. It displayed passages from his favorite mystery novelist, side-by-side with transcripts from a 1990s true crime television program. The dialogue and narration were identical. Lin stood at the front of the room. "The author copied the television scripts word for word," she stated to the class. Arthur raised his hand and noted that the novels were published globally to wide commercial success. Lin responded that the legal proceedings were currently ongoing. Arthur took out his yellow highlighter. He drew lines over the identical text blocks on the paper. He closed his notebook and placed the pen in his bag. The classroom clock indicated it was two o'clock. Arthur gathered his belongings, walked out of the door, and headed down the hallway toward the science building.

I turned on the Bluetooth speaker in my living room and selected an investigative journalism podcast. The host was analyzing the career of my preferred science fiction writer, Thomas Aris. According to the broadcast, Aris utilized software to scrape text from amateur web forums, rearranging the character names before publishing the works as original novels. The host interviewed a programmer who explained how the software functioned. I paused the audio and called my friend, Sarah. When she answered, I told her about the podcast's findings regarding Aris. "I just bought his newest release yesterday," she said over the phone. I suggested that she could return it to the retailer with her receipt. I ended the call, placed the phone on the coffee table, and resumed the podcast. I listened to the remaining twenty minutes while I folded my laundry and placed it in the basket.

Sylvia stood in line at the bookstore holding a hardcover copy of The Silver Locket. She overheard two employees talking near the register. One employee mentioned that the publisher had just issued a recall for the author's entire catalog due to confirmed plagiarism from public domain stories. Sylvia stepped out of the line and walked over to the employees. "Are you returning all copies to the distributor?" she asked. The taller employee confirmed that they were packing the boxes today. Sylvia looked at the book in her hands. The author, whom she had read exclusively for five years, was sitting at a table at the front of the store. A store manager approached the table and spoke to the author in low tones. Sylvia placed the hardcover on a nearby display shelf. She turned around, exited through the sliding doors, and walked to her car.

Marcus placed The Crimson Horizon next to an older novel titled Red Skies. He ran his index finger down the first page of both books. The sentence structure and vocabulary were identical in twenty consecutive paragraphs. His favorite author, Julian Vance, had published The Crimson Horizon three years after Red Skies was released. Marcus looked up at the librarian. He asked if he could check out both books for two weeks. "Standard lending rules apply to all materials," she replied, scanning the barcodes. Marcus put the books in his canvas bag and walked out of the building. Once outside, he took out his phone and opened Vance's social media page. Marcus typed a comment stating that the text matched the older book verbatim. He pressed the send button, put his phone away, and continued walking down the street toward the bus stop.

I open the mobile application while waiting for the bus at the corner of Elm and 4th Street. A red indicator shows one new friend request. The profile belongs to Sarah Jenkins. During middle school, Sarah told other students that I did not wash my clothes. I tap the screen to view her profile picture, which shows her standing next to a white sedan. "Is this the downtown bus?" a man asks, pointing down the street. I tell him that it is. I return my attention to the phone screen. I press the 'Accept' button. A new message window opens automatically. Sarah types a message saying she is visiting the city next week. I type a response stating I currently live in the north district. The bus arrives. I put the phone in my jacket pocket and board the vehicle.

The tablet rests on the kitchen counter next to a bowl of apples. Elena wipes the surface with a damp cloth. A chime sounds from the device. She picks it up and sees an alert from a networking site. David Vance has sent a connection request. David pushed Elena into the mud behind the gymnasium twelve years ago. Her roommate, Chloe, enters the kitchen carrying a cardboard box. Chloe mentions that the mail has arrived. Elena acknowledges the information. She taps David's profile. His current occupation is listed as a regional manager for a logistics company. "Who is messaging you?" Chloe asks while sorting the envelopes. Elena says it is a connection request from a former classmate. Elena locks the tablet screen without accepting or rejecting the request. She places the device back on the counter and picks up an apple.

My laptop screen illuminates the dark room. I navigate to the pending requests tab. Gregory Miller's name appears at the top of the list. In high school, Gregory frequently knocked my books off my desk. I open a new browser tab and search for his name. The results show he owns a landscaping business in Ohio. My phone rings on the bedside table. I answer it. My brother asks if I am coming to dinner on Friday. I confirm that I will be there by six o'clock. We end the call. I switch back to the social media tab. I click the button to delete Gregory's request. The interface updates to show zero pending requests. I close the laptop, turn off the desk lamp, and walk to the kitchen to pour a glass of water from the tap.

Arthur stands in line at the grocery store. He holds a basket containing bread, milk, and eggs. He retrieves his phone from his pocket. A banner notification indicates a friend request from Kevin Barnes. Kevin threw Arthur's backpack into the school swimming pool when they were teenagers. The cashier announces that register four is open. Arthur walks to the register and places his items on the conveyor belt. He looks at his phone again. Kevin has sent an accompanying message stating he would like to catch up. Arthur pays for his groceries using a credit card. He tells the cashier to have a good day, and the cashier replies with a similar statement. Arthur walks out through the automatic doors. He types a message back to Kevin saying his schedule is full. He sends the message and unlocks his car.

The smartwatch on my wrist vibrates twice. I look at the screen. The notification shows a friend request from Melissa Thorne. Melissa cut my hair with scissors during an art class when we were eight years old. I tap the notification to expand it. Her profile lists a mutual connection, my cousin Paul. I walk into the living room where my wife is folding laundry. She asks if I have fed the dog. I reply that I fed the dog at five o'clock. I use the watch interface to send a message to Paul. I ask Paul how he knows Melissa. Paul replies within one minute, stating they work in the same office building. I look at the friend request again. I select the option to ignore the request. I sit on the sofa and turn on the television.

I am painting the baseboards in the hallway. My phone rings on the drop cloth. I wipe my hands on a rag and pick up the device. The screen displays an email alert for a social media request. The sender is Vanessa Hayes. Vanessa drew on my assignments with a permanent marker in the fifth grade. I open the link. Her page displays her current location as Seattle. My neighbor knocks on the open front door. He says he is borrowing the ladder from the garage. I tell him to make sure he locks the garage when he is done. I look down at the phone. I press the option to hide the notification. I place the phone back on the drop cloth. I pick up the paintbrush, dip it into the white paint, and resume painting the baseboards.

I sit on the park bench eating a sandwich. I unlock my phone to check the weather forecast. A social media icon shows a notification badge. I open the application. The friend request is from Bradley Cooper. Bradley threw rocks at my bicycle tires when we lived in the same neighborhood. A pigeon lands on the pavement near my feet. I throw a small piece of bread to the pigeon. The bird eats it. I look at Bradley's profile. There are photographs of a house and a dog. "Are you using this space?" a jogger asks, pointing to the other end of the bench. I tell him the space is available. The jogger sits down to tie his shoelace. I press the block button on Bradley's profile. The application returns to the home feed. I finish my sandwich.

Victor sits in the airport terminal waiting for his flight to Denver. He connects his laptop to the public Wi-Fi network. A pop-up window shows a new friend request from Simon Reed. Simon locked Victor in a locker during their seventh-grade physical education class. The intercom announces that boarding for flight 402 will begin in fifteen minutes. Victor looks at the screen. He clicks on Simon's message. Simon asks if Victor still lives in Chicago. The passenger sitting next to Victor asks for the time. "It is two-thirty," Victor states. Victor begins typing a response to Simon. He writes that he moved away from Chicago five years ago. He sends the message and accepts the request. Victor unplugs his laptop charger from the wall outlet and places the computer into his black carry-on bag.

Karen drinks coffee at the diner. She scrolls through her social media feed on her phone. A pending request appears from Jason Brooks. Jason put chewing gum in Karen's hair during a field trip to the science museum. The waitress walks to the table and pours more coffee into Karen's mug. Karen thanks the waitress. The waitress asks if Karen wants the breakfast menu. Karen declines and says she is only having coffee. She looks at Jason's profile. It shows he is employed as a mechanic. She selects the option to accept the friend request. Jason's status changes to 'Connected'. Karen pays her bill, leaving three dollars on the table for the tip. She puts her phone in her purse, walks out of the diner, and starts the engine of her truck.

I open my email inbox while sitting at the kitchen table. The system shows a connection request from a professional networking site. The name on the request is Michael Trent. Michael frequently took my pencils and broke them during our math class. I click the profile link. Michael is seeking employment in the marketing sector. The oven timer beeps. I stand up and turn off the timer. I take the baking sheet out of the oven. I put the sheet on the stove. I return to the computer. I type a message to Michael. "My company is not currently hiring," I write. I send the message and decline the connection request. I close the email application and walk back to the stove to transfer the baked goods to a cooling rack.

Diana reviews her emails at the library. The third email is an automated notification from an alumni network. Someone named Richard Cole has requested to add her to his contact list. Richard tripped Diana in the hallway every morning during their sophomore year. Diana clicks the link in the email. The webpage loads Richard's profile. He has uploaded a resume detailing his experience in software development. A librarian approaches and asks Diana to lower the brightness of her screen. Diana complies and says she will keep it dim. She looks at the 'Accept' and 'Decline' buttons below Richard's name. She clicks 'Accept'. A confirmation message appears on the screen. Diana logs out of the alumni network. She closes the web browser, gathers her notebooks, and walks toward the exit of the library.

Mark sits at his desktop computer in a gray office cubicle. The screen displays a notification from a social media platform. He clicks the icon. The text reads, "Friend Request: Tom Harris." Mark looks at the name. Tom Harris took Mark's lunch box repeatedly during the fourth grade. Mark types a message to his coworker, asking if she has seen the latest quarterly report. She replies that she sent it ten minutes ago. Mark reads her reply, then looks back at the friend request. "I am going to decline this," Mark states aloud to the empty cubicle. He clicks the 'Decline' button. The notification disappears from the screen. Mark opens the quarterly report document and begins reading the financial projections for the upcoming fiscal year, taking notes with a black pen on a yellow notepad.

A wicker basket wrapped in clear plastic sat on the porch of the townhouse. Julian picked up the basket and read the attached paper tag. The name printed on the tag was Fiona Gallagher. Julian checked his records and noted that Fiona was the prior tenant. At noon, the mail carrier arrived at the end of the street. Julian walked down the sidewalk carrying the basket. He informed the mail carrier that the item had been left at his house for the previous occupant. The carrier inspected the paper tag. "This did not come through the postal system," the carrier said. Julian asked how he should proceed. The carrier suggested contacting the local florist shop listed at the bottom of the tag. Julian said he would make the phone call, and he carried the basket back to his porch.

I opened the door of my industrial loft and found a flat, rectangular package leaning against the doorframe. The shipping label indicated it was sent to Martin Reed. Martin Reed held the lease on this loft before I moved in. I saw a delivery driver wearing a brown uniform walking toward the freight elevator. I called out to him, stating that he had left a package for the wrong person. The driver stopped and turned around. "The address on the label matches your door number," he said. I explained that the address was correct, but the recipient no longer lived in the building. I handed the package back to the driver. He scanned the barcode with his mobile device and said he would mark it as undeliverable. I watched him enter the freight elevator before closing my door.

A delivery drone hovered above the patio of the desert home and lowered a white box onto the tiles. Nora stepped outside as the drone retracted its tether and flew away. She looked at the digital manifest on the side of the box. The recipient was Leonard Vance, the previous occupant of the property. Nora pressed the button on her wrist communicator to contact the local distribution hub. She reported that a drone had dropped a package for a former resident. The dispatcher asked for the serial number on the manifest. "The serial number is seven seven two," Nora said. The dispatcher stated that a retrieval drone would be dispatched in twenty minutes to collect the box. Nora replied that she would leave the box on the patio. She went back inside the house and secured the glass door.

I unlocked the mailbox designated for my apartment in the college town. A textbook-sized parcel wrapped in brown paper was crammed inside. I pulled the parcel out and inspected the front. The name written in black marker was Chloe Simmons. Chloe was the student who rented the apartment during the previous academic year. I carried the parcel to the leasing office on the ground floor. I set it on the desk of the administrative assistant. I stated that the parcel was delivered to my box but addressed to the former tenant. The assistant checked a digital database on her monitor. "She left a forwarding address in another state," the assistant said. I asked if the office would mail it to her. The assistant confirmed that they would handle the shipping process. I left the parcel on the desk and exited the leasing office.

A delivery van parked outside the mountain cabin. A courier walked up the gravel path carrying a sealed metal case. Victor opened the door and signed the electronic clipboard. After the courier returned to the van, Victor examined the case. The tag identified the recipient as Dr. Aris Thorne. Victor checked his property records and saw that Dr. Thorne was the previous owner. Victor walked down the path and signaled for the van to stop. He told the courier that he had signed in error. The courier rolled down the window. "I can reverse the delivery scan," the courier said. Victor handed the metal case through the window and confirmed that this was an acceptable solution. The courier adjusted the status on the clipboard and drove away.

I returned to my suburban duplex at five o'clock and saw a heavy, square box sitting on the front steps. The delivery sticker showed my street address, but the name on the first line was Gregory Evans. I recognized the name as the person who lived here before my tenancy began. My neighbor, Robert, was watering the lawn in the adjacent yard. I walked over to the property line. I pointed at the box and told Robert that a package for Gregory had arrived. Robert turned off his hose. "Gregory moved to a house on Elm Street," Robert said. I asked Robert if he knew the exact house number. He stated that Gregory lived at number forty-two. I said I would drive the box over to Elm Street later in the evening. Robert nodded, coiled his hose, and walked into his garage.

Elena stepped onto the wooden deck of her beachside rental property. A gray plastic shipping bag was wedged between the screen door and the exterior wall. She pulled the bag free and read the shipping information. The recipient was listed as Thomas Aris, the individual who rented the house last season. Elena took her phone from her pocket and called the property owner. When the owner answered, Elena explained the situation regarding the misdirected package. The owner asked if the bag had a return address. "There is a return address printed in the upper left corner," Elena said. The owner instructed Elena to leave the bag on the kitchen counter, adding that a property manager would retrieve it on Tuesday. Elena said she understood the instructions. She walked into the kitchen, placed the plastic bag on the granite counter, and ended the phone call.

I entered the mailroom of my condo building to retrieve my letters. Inside my locker, I found a cylindrical cardboard tube alongside two billing statements. The label on the tube bore the name Michael Chang. Michael Chang occupied my unit before I signed the lease. I carried the tube to the concierge desk near the main entrance. The concierge, a woman in a black uniform, was typing on a computer. I said, "This item was placed in locker 4B, but it belongs to the previous resident." She stopped typing and took the tube from my hand. She informed me that she would contact the delivery service to arrange a pickup. I told her I appreciated the assistance. She placed the tube on a shelf behind her chair, and I walked out the glass doors toward the street.

Marcus drove his pickup truck to the end of the dirt driveway and stopped next to the aluminum mailbox. A large cardboard box sat on the ground near the wooden post. Marcus picked up the box and placed it in the bed of his truck. The shipping label listed the address of his rural farmhouse, but the recipient was Julian Vance. Marcus drove to the local post office in the center of town. He carried the box inside and placed it on the counter. He told the clerk that the package was meant for the man who lived at the farm three years ago. The clerk scanned the barcode with a handheld device. "We will return this to the sender," the clerk said. Marcus replied that returning it was the correct procedure. He exited the post office and returned to his vehicle in the parking lot.

I found a padded yellow envelope lying on the welcome mat outside my city apartment. I bent down and picked it up. The printed text on the front indicated it was addressed to Sarah Jenkins, the woman who leased the unit before me. I walked down the carpeted hallway and took the elevator to the lobby. The building manager, David, was standing behind the reception desk. I handed the envelope to him and explained that it belonged to the previous tenant. David looked at the label. "I have her forwarding address in the filing cabinet," he said. I told him that I would let him handle the forwarding process. David placed the envelope on the desk surface and stated he would mail it out with the afternoon post. I nodded, turned around, and took the elevator back up to my floor.

Clara walked out of her front door and saw a wooden crate resting on the concrete steps. The shipping label displayed the address of her suburban house, but the recipient name read Arthur Pendelton. Clara knew Arthur was the previous owner of the property. She picked up her cellular phone and dialed the number for the logistics company printed on the side of the crate. A representative answered the call. Clara stated that a package had been delivered to the correct address but the wrong person. The representative asked her to read the tracking number aloud. "The number is four eight two nine," Clara said. The representative instructed her to leave the crate on the porch. Clara said she would do so. She placed the wooden crate back onto the concrete steps and returned inside her house, closing the front door behind her.

A dock worker approached my floating houseboat and handed me a yellow waterproof bag. I looked at the name tag attached to the zipper. The bag was designated for Elias Vance, the man who owned the houseboat before I purchased it. I walked along the wooden pier until I reached the harbor master's office. I entered the building and placed the bag on the counter. I told the harbor master that the bag was delivered to my boat, but it was meant for Elias Vance. The harbor master picked up the bag. "Elias docked his new vessel at pier seven," the harbor master said. I suggested that the office staff could deliver it to him. The harbor master agreed to transfer the bag to pier seven during his afternoon rounds. I left the office and walked back along the pier to my houseboat.

Brenda stood behind the checkout counter reading a letter delivered by the morning post. It was from a woman who had shoplifted merchandise from the boutique twelve years ago. The letter included a money order for fifty dollars. The writer stated, "I apologize for taking the items without paying. Please accept this compensation." Brenda placed the money order inside the cash register. A customer approached the counter carrying two garments on hangers. The customer asked if the store offered alterations. Brenda replied that alterations were available on Thursdays. She processed the transaction, bagged the clothing, and handed the receipt to the customer. After the customer left, Brenda took a paperclip from a small container and attached the apology letter to the daily sales log. She then began folding the displayed sweaters on the adjacent table.

Dr. Lin found a hand-addressed letter in her faculty pigeonhole. The sender was listed as David Thorne, a student from a seminar she taught eight years ago. Sitting at her office desk, she unfolded the stationery. David wrote, "I apologize for misattributing the primary sources in my final dissertation. My methodology was flawed." Dr. Lin noted the date at the top of the page. She picked up her telephone and dialed the department secretary. When the secretary answered, Dr. Lin requested that her upcoming lecture notes be printed. The secretary confirmed the request and asked if there were any updates to the syllabus. Dr. Lin stated that the syllabus remained unchanged. She placed David's letter in the paper shredder beside her desk. The machine activated, cutting the paper into thin strips. Dr. Lin then opened her laptop to begin work.

I sat at the corner table of the cafe with an espresso and a letter forwarded by my previous landlord. The signature at the bottom belonged to Elena, my former business partner from a decade ago. The text contained an apology. "I am sorry for selling the retail space without consulting you first," it read. I took a sip of the coffee and placed the cup back on the saucer. The waiter approached the table to clear the empty plates. He asked if I needed anything else. I told him I would like the check. I read the letter one more time before putting it into my briefcase. I left the payment on the table, picked up the briefcase, and exited the cafe. I walked down the street toward the subway station to commute to my current workplace.

Marcus wiped motor oil from his hands using a shop rag and picked up the piece of mail resting on his toolbox. It was a letter from a supplier, dated five years after their last transaction. The typed note stated, "We apologize for the defective brake pads shipped to your garage in 2019. The manufacturing error has since been identified." Marcus set the letter down and walked over to the inspection bay. His apprentice, Leo, was examining a vehicle's suspension. Leo pointed at the chassis and mentioned that the struts needed replacement. Marcus agreed with the assessment and told Leo to order the standard parts. Marcus returned to the toolbox, slid the supplier's letter into a plastic sleeve, and pinned it to the corkboard on the wall. He then picked up a wrench to continue working on the engine block.

I rode the southbound commuter train and read a letter I had received in the morning mail. It was sent by a contractor who had renovated my kitchen eleven years ago. The printed text contained an apology regarding the materials used. "I am apologizing for installing substandard plumbing fixtures under your sink," the contractor wrote. I placed the paper on my lap. The ticket inspector walked down the aisle checking fares. He stopped at my row and asked to see my monthly pass. I presented the pass and stated that the train was operating on schedule today. He confirmed this fact, clipped my ticket, and moved to the next passenger. I put the letter back into the envelope, placed it in my briefcase, and looked out the window at the passing industrial buildings as the train advanced.

I waited in the clinic lobby while reviewing a letter forwarded by my insurance provider. The sender was a physical therapist I had seen nine years ago for a knee injury. The letter contained an admission of error regarding my treatment plan. "I am writing to apologize for prescribing the incorrect strengthening exercises," the text read. The receptionist called my name from behind the glass partition. I approached her desk. She stated that the doctor was ready to see me and asked for my current identification card. I handed her the card and told her that my address remained the same. She returned the card to me. I slipped the apology letter into my folder of medical records, picked up my coat, and walked down the hallway toward examination room three to wait for the physician.

Julian sat at a reading table in the public library and unsealed an envelope. The document inside was a formal apology from the city council regarding a zoning dispute from a decade earlier. The letter read, "The council apologizes for the improper confiscation of the community garden parcel in 2014." Julian scanned the page and set it beside his stack of reference books. The librarian walked down the aisle and paused at his table. She informed him that the library would be closing in fifteen minutes. Julian acknowledged the information and asked if he could check out the encyclopedias. The librarian told him that reference materials could not leave the building. Julian nodded, packed the city council's letter into his backpack, and returned the heavy books to their designated shelf before heading toward the exit.

I collected the mail from the metal box at the end of the dirt driveway. Among the catalogs was an envelope with a return address from Arizona. I carried it to the kitchen and used a butter knife to open it. The letter was from Mark. He stated that he was apologizing for leaving the gate open six years ago, which allowed the horses to exit the pasture. "I take full responsibility for the property damage," he wrote. I placed the letter on the granite countertop. I called my brother to inform him about the mail. He asked what Mark had written. I told him that Mark took responsibility for the incident. I folded the letter along its original creases, put it back into the envelope, and set it next to the coffee maker. I proceeded to prepare my lunch.

I sat on a wooden bench in the municipal park and opened the envelope I had carried from my apartment. The letter was from an individual who had crashed into my bicycle seven years prior. The handwriting was legible in black ink. "I apologize for not stopping after the collision on 4th Street," the person wrote. I observed a jogger passing by on the paved path. A municipal worker in a high-visibility vest stopped his golf cart nearby. He asked if the trash can next to the bench was full. I looked at the receptacle and informed him that it was only half full. The worker thanked me and drove away. I folded the letter in half, placed it in my jacket pocket, and stood up. I began walking along the path toward the park exit to return home.

Arthur retrieved a sealed envelope from his mailbox at the accounting firm. The postmark indicated it was mailed from Chicago three days prior. Inside was a single sheet of lined paper. The text read, "I am writing to apologize for the calculation error I made in the 2018 quarterly report. I should have double-checked the spreadsheet before submission." Arthur read the words twice, then placed the paper on his desk next to his keyboard. His colleague, a woman named Sarah, walked past and asked if he had received the pending tax documents. Arthur replied that the letter was from a former employee regarding an old file. He opened the top drawer of his filing cabinet, placed the letter inside a folder marked 'Correspondence', and closed the drawer. He returned to his computer and typed a response to a client email.

I sat at the boarding gate in the airport, holding a letter from my former neighbor. The envelope was postmarked from a different country. The neighbor was writing about an incident that occurred fourteen years ago regarding property lines. "I apologize for cutting down the oak tree on your side of the fence," the letter stated. I read the sentence and turned the page over to see if there was writing on the back. It was blank. The airline agent announced over the loudspeaker that flight 402 was ready for boarding. A passenger next to me asked if they were boarding group A yet. I told her that they were currently boarding passengers requiring assistance. I placed the letter into my carry-on bag, stood up, and joined the queue forming at the counter.

Foreman Miller stood by the cement mixer holding a piece of mail forwarded from the main office. The letter was signed by a former subcontractor who had worked on a housing project fifteen years ago. The handwritten note stated, "I apologize for abandoning the job site prior to the completion of the foundational work." Miller folded the letter and put it into his hard hat before placing the hat on his head. A surveyor approached with a tripod over his shoulder. The surveyor mentioned that the ground measurements were complete and asked where to store the equipment. Miller instructed him to put the tools in the green storage container. The surveyor walked toward the container. Miller picked up his clipboard and began checking off the inventory list for the day's delivery of steel beams.

I held onto the overhead rail as the subway train moved through the tunnel. My phone vibrated in my jacket pocket. I pulled it out and unlocked the screen to see a notification from a social media application. A former classmate had added me to a group titled "Lincoln High 5-Year Reunion." I scrolled through the event description. The reunion was planned for the second weekend of July at a local park. A passenger sitting in front of me asked if the next stop was Central Station. I told him that Central Station was three stops away. "Thank you for the information," the passenger said. I returned my attention to the phone screen and marked my attendance status as pending. The train decelerated, and I put the device back into my pocket before the doors opened.

Arthur drove his tractor to the edge of the cornfield and stopped the engine. He walked to the metal mailbox located on Route 9. Among the agricultural catalogs was a blue envelope addressed in silver ink. It was an invitation to the Westbridge High School fiftieth reunion. Arthur walked back to the farmhouse and placed the envelope on the dining table. His wife, Martha, poured a glass of water and handed it to him. She asked who the blue envelope was from. Arthur stated that the alumni committee was holding a gathering in the school cafeteria. "The date is set for September second," Arthur said, pointing at the printed text. Martha noted that September second was a Tuesday. Arthur drank the water, left the envelope on the wood surface, and returned outside to repair the perimeter fence.

I inserted the brass key into P.O. Box 402 and turned it to the right. Inside the metal compartment was a single piece of mail. It was a postcard from the Washington High Alumni Board, announcing a fifteen-year class reunion. I walked to the post office counter where the clerk was weighing a package. I asked the clerk if I could borrow a pen. "There is a blue pen attached to the clipboard on the side table," the clerk said. I thanked him and went to the side table. I wrote my current mailing address on the RSVP section of the postcard. I checked the box indicating that I would attend the dinner portion of the event. I detached the return portion, handed it to the clerk for processing, and exited the building through the glass doors.

Dr. Aris sat in the clinic breakroom eating a sandwich. The receptionist, Brenda, walked in and placed a stack of sorted mail on the table. One envelope had the emblem of Northside Secondary School printed in the corner. Aris opened it using a plastic knife. The enclosed letter was an invitation to a twenty-five-year class reunion. Brenda poured coffee into a ceramic mug and asked what the letter said. Aris told her that his former high school was hosting an alumni event at the end of the month. "It says there will be a catered lunch and a tour of the new science wing," Aris said. Brenda stated that the clinic would be closed on that specific weekend. Aris folded the letter into thirds, placed it next to his sandwich, and resumed eating his lunch in silence.

Julian wiped motor oil from his hands using a red rag. He walked to the office area of the auto repair shop. On his desk sat a piece of mail forwarded from his previous address. He tore open the top edge and pulled out a card. It was an invitation to his high school class reunion, scheduled for the upcoming spring. His business partner, Greg, entered the office holding a wrench. Greg asked Julian if the parts for the transmission had arrived. Julian replied that the supplier would deliver the parts tomorrow morning. "What did you get in the mail?" Greg asked, gesturing with the wrench. Julian explained that it was an announcement for a high school gathering. He placed the card in the top drawer of his metal desk, closed the drawer, and walked back to the garage bay.

I stood backstage and tuned my guitar. The venue manager walked past and handed me a letter that had been sent to the club. I opened the envelope and found a formal invitation to the Springfield High ten-year reunion. The paper detailed a schedule of events, including a morning assembly and an evening dance. The sound engineer spoke through the monitor speakers, asking me to play a chord for a volume check. I strummed the strings once. "The levels look balanced," the engineer said. I told him I would be ready to perform in five minutes. I looked back at the reunion invitation, noting the RSVP deadline was three weeks away. I folded the paper in half and slid it into the front pocket of my guitar case. I then adjusted my microphone stand to the correct height.

Elena stood behind the espresso machine when the postal worker entered the cafe. The worker handed her a thick cream-colored envelope. Elena placed it next to the cash register and finished pouring milk into a cup. Later, when the shop was empty, she inspected the envelope. It contained a formal invitation to the Riverside High twenty-year reunion. Her employee, Thomas, swept the floor nearby. Thomas asked if she had received an important letter. Elena explained that it was a notice for a high school gathering. "They rented out the country club for the dinner," she said, reading the itinerary printed on the card. Thomas mentioned that country clubs usually have strict dress codes. Elena nodded and placed the invitation in her apron pocket. She picked up a damp cloth and began wiping the stainless steel counter.

Chloe sat at a wooden table in the university library. She connected her laptop to the public wireless network and opened her email application. The first unread message was a digital invitation to her fifteen-year high school reunion. The email contained a link to purchase tickets and a map of the event location. The student sitting across from her leaned forward. He asked if she was using the outlet beneath the table. Chloe told him that her laptop was running on battery power and the outlet was available. "I appreciate it," the student said, plugging in a white power adapter. Chloe clicked the link in the email to view the ticket prices. The cost was listed as seventy-five dollars per person. She closed the browser window, opened her research document, and began typing a summary of the academic journal article.

I walked up the stairs to my apartment on the third floor. A green envelope was wedged between the door and the doorframe. I pulled it out and unlocked the deadbolt. Inside the apartment, I opened the envelope and extracted a card. It was an invitation to the Valley High School thirty-year reunion. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, stepped out into the hallway and locked his door. He asked if I had seen the building superintendent today. I told him that I saw the superintendent in the basement yesterday afternoon. "I need him to check my radiator," Mr. Henderson said. I told him to leave a written request in the lobby drop-box. I stepped inside my apartment and closed the door. I placed the green envelope on the entryway table and removed my winter coat, hanging it in the closet.

I sat at my office desk and refreshed my email inbox. A new message appeared from the sender "Class of 2014." The subject line indicated it was an invitation to our ten-year reunion. I clicked on the email to view the details. The text stated the reunion would take place at a hotel downtown, requiring a fifty-dollar entry fee. My coworker, Sarah, walked past my cubicle and stopped. She asked me what I was reading on my monitor. I told her that my high school was organizing a reunion event for next month. "You should buy a ticket," Sarah said while holding a stack of printing paper. I replied that I would consider the logistics of traveling back to my hometown. I closed the email tab, opened a spreadsheet, and resumed typing data into the cells.

Mark opened the mailbox at the end of his driveway. Inside was a white envelope with a return address from Oak Creek High School Alumni Association. He walked back to his house and placed the envelope on the kitchen counter. His roommate, David, was chopping carrots. David asked what came in the mail. Mark said it was an invitation to their ten-year high school reunion. He then opened the envelope and read the printed card. The event was scheduled for October 14th at the municipal gymnasium. "Are you going to attend?" David asked. Mark folded the card and placed it back into the envelope. He told David he needed to check his work schedule before making a decision. He then walked to his bedroom and turned on his computer.

I taped a cardboard box shut and carried it to the living room. The mail carrier dropped a bundle of envelopes through the slot in the front door. I picked them up from the floor and sorted through them. One envelope was a glossy invitation to the Central High School graduating class of 2004 reunion. I read the location, which was a banquet hall two states away. The moving company driver knocked on the open door frame. He asked if the stack of boxes in the hallway was ready to be loaded into the truck. I told him that those boxes were completely packed and sealed. "I will start loading them now," the driver said. I placed the reunion invitation into a folder labeled 'miscellaneous documents,' put the folder inside my backpack, and picked up a roll of packing tape.

I unlocked the front door of the bakery at 4:00 AM and found a bunch of lavender tied with twine on the floormat. I picked up the lavender and stepped inside, locking the door behind me. I turned on the overhead lights. I examined the twine knot and the stems. There was no card or paper attached. My business partner, Clara, emerged from the back room carrying a tray of flour. I showed her the lavender. Clara asked if anyone was outside. "The street is empty," I replied. I walked over to the display case and set the lavender on top of the glass counter. I tied my apron strings behind my back and went to the industrial mixer. I poured a bag of sugar into the bowl and pressed the green button to start the machine for the first batch of dough.

A delivery person in a brown uniform placed a glass vase containing twelve white lilies on Mark’s desk at 10:14 AM. Mark stopped typing on his keyboard and inspected the stems and the water. He rotated the vase 360 degrees. There was no envelope or card attached to the arrangement. Mark stood up and walked to the adjacent cubicle. He asked Sarah if she had seen who ordered the delivery. Sarah stated that she had been looking at her monitor and did not notice anything. "I will leave them on the corner of the desk," Mark said. He returned to his chair, moved the vase to the upper right corner of his workstation, and resumed typing on his spreadsheet. The flowers remained there for the rest of the workday, and the water level dropped slightly by 5:00 PM.

Nurse Peterson carried a plastic container of pink carnations into Room 412. The patient, Mr. Hayes, was sitting upright in his bed, watching the wall clock. Peterson set the container on the rolling tray table. Mr. Hayes asked who sent the floral arrangement. Peterson explained that she did not know, as they were dropped off at the front desk without a delivery tag. "Look for a small envelope," Mr. Hayes said. Peterson separated the carnations with her fingers and checked the plastic wrapping. She informed him that there was absolutely nothing attached to the stems or the base. Mr. Hayes nodded once and instructed her to push the tray table closer to the window. Peterson unlocked the wheels, moved the table against the windowsill, and recorded Mr. Hayes's blood pressure on the chart before exiting the room to check on the next patient.

A woman wearing a green apron walked into my hardware store holding a bundle of red roses. She set them on the checkout counter next to the cash register and left without speaking. I picked up the roses and examined the packaging. There was a barcode on the plastic wrap, but no greeting card or sender information. I asked my manager, who was restocking batteries nearby, if he had ordered them. He told me he had not made any purchases today. "I will put them in a bucket of water," I said. I retrieved a plastic bucket from aisle four, filled it at the utility sink, and placed the roses inside. I set the bucket near the front entrance, next to the display of gardening gloves. A customer approached the register with a box of nails, and I proceeded to scan the barcode to complete the transaction.

The prep cook carried a glass vase of purple orchids through the swinging kitchen doors and set it on the stainless steel prep table. Chef Lin looked up from cutting a salmon fillet. The prep cook mentioned that a courier had left the vase at the rear loading dock ten minutes prior. Lin washed her hands at the sink and dried them with a paper towel. She inspected the vase and the surrounding leaves. "Find the card," Lin instructed. The prep cook lifted the vase and checked underneath it, then stated that the courier had not provided one. Lin told him to move the arrangement to the manager's office so it would not interfere with the food preparation area. The prep cook carried the orchids down the hallway, while Lin picked up her knife and made another incision along the spine of the fish.

I was sitting on bench four at the train station when a person in a grey coat walked past and handed me a bundle of daisies. Before I could speak, the person boarded the departing northbound train. I looked at the stems, which were bound by a single rubber band. I checked the leaves and stems for any attached notes. There was no paper or card. I turned to the ticket inspector standing nearby and asked if he knew the individual in the grey coat. The inspector said he had not observed the interaction. "They just handed these to me," I stated. I placed the daisies on the wooden slats of the bench next to my briefcase. The automated speaker announced the arrival of the southbound train. I picked up my briefcase, leaving the daisies on the bench, and walked toward the edge of the platform.

I unlocked my front door and noticed a bouquet of yellow tulips wrapped in brown paper resting on the welcome mat. I picked up the bundle and searched through the overlapping layers of paper. There was no card or receipt tucked inside. I brought the flowers into the kitchen, where my roommate, David, was chopping carrots. I told him that I found these outside. David asked if there was a name on them. "There is no card," I replied. I filled a ceramic pitcher with tap water and used kitchen shears to trim the ends of the stems by one inch. I placed the tulips into the pitcher and set it on the center of the dining table. David finished chopping the carrots and swept them into a stainless steel pot on the stove. I walked to the living room to turn on the television.

A local florist delivery driver approached the library circulation desk and placed a square glass vase filled with blue hydrangeas on the counter. He required a signature on his digital tablet. I signed my name with my index finger, and the driver exited through the sliding glass doors. I picked up the vase and rotated it, looking for a recipient name. There was no card, envelope, or sticker on the glass. I turned to my supervisor, Elena, who was scanning returned books. I informed her about the delivery and the missing information. Elena told me to check the delivery log on the computer. I typed the time of arrival into the system. "There are no scheduled deliveries today," I said. I placed the hydrangeas on top of the reference section cabinet. I then returned to the desk and began sorting a stack of paperbacks by author last name.

A mail carrier walked into the auto repair garage holding a bundle of white baby's breath wrapped in clear cellophane. He handed the bundle to Greg, who was wiping oil off a wrench with a rag. The carrier stated that the package was addressed to the shop's street number. Greg set his wrench down and inspected the cellophane. He turned the bundle over twice. He pointed out to the carrier that there was no name or card attached. The carrier stated he was only required to deliver it to the address. "Put it on the counter," Greg said to his apprentice, Tom. Tom took the flowers and laid them flat on the billing counter next to the cash register. Greg wiped his hands again, picked up his flashlight, and walked back under the lifted chassis of a silver sedan to finish draining the transmission fluid.

A taxi pulled up to the main entrance of the hotel, and the driver brought a tall arrangement of bird of paradise flowers to the front desk. The driver said a passenger had left them in the backseat and asked him to drop them off here. I accepted the arrangement and placed it on the marble counter. I searched the stems, the base of the vase, and the leaves for a card. There was no writing or identifying marker of any kind. I asked the bellhop if he recognized the taxi. He replied that it was a standard city cab. "I will leave them in the lobby," I said. I carried the arrangement to the center table in the waiting area and set it between two leather armchairs. I walked back to the front desk and began printing the arrival manifest for the afternoon guests.
